9B7E989FCE3A45E38DA9BAEC0F177F63.description: Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., ask for clarification or repetition) using learned phrases (e.g., Could you repeat that please? I believe…) and open responses to express and defend opinions.

643553ED0ABB4BCC8B3D5454EDFE258A.description: Offering and justifying opinions, negotiating with and persuading others in communicative exchanges

A75E7D49680248CF9536BE7B98ABA84F.description: Collaborate with peers to engage in a variety of extended written exchanges and complex grade-appropriate writing projects, using technology as appropriate.

1330F5949C2249519C0BDAD412343219.description: Collaborate with peers to engage in increasingly complex grade-appropriate written exchanges and writing projects, using technology as appropriate.

E10A8B08F2694B24BDA92AFB7D464B17.description: Collaborate with peers to engage in short, grade-appropriate written exchanges and writing projects, using technology as appropriate.

774502F6D4484BFB82449FE5D28A7411.description: Interacting with others in written English in various communicative forms (print, communicative technology, and multimedia)

B9C0DE6484D743F59DA0007885AF5EC2.description: Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions, sustaining conversations on a variety of age and grade-appropriate academic topics by following turn-taking rules, asking and answering relevant, on-topic questions, affirming others, and providing coherent and well-articulated comments and additional information.

6E8A8CFFBFBC4A918110CBEB51B53512.description: Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions, sustaining conversations on a variety of age and grade-appropriate academic topics by following turn-taking rules, asking and answering relevant, on-topic questions, affirming others, providing additional, relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

0AFBB2EDA5314590AF307DBA18627554.description: Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar current events and academic topics by asking and answering yes-no questions and wh- questions and responding using phrases and short sentences.

31C5384DE51348AA88038A20545044E3.description: Exchanging information and ideas with others through oral collaborative discussions on a range of social and academic topics

document.title: Next Generation Science Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten through Grade Twelve

8FC618428E624294B6F5F025E681D6E6.description: Construct an argument with evidence that some changes caused by heating or cooling can be reversed and some cannot.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of reversible changes could include materials such as water and butter at different temperatures. Examples of irreversible changes could include cooking an egg, freezing a plant leaf, and heating paper.

53F76C76A93C48558F064C76F7E37ABD.description: Make observations to construct an evidence-based account of how an object made of a small set of pieces can be disassembled and made into a new object.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of pieces could include blocks, building bricks, or other assorted small objects.

27A7AAF8D9184B0DBF25CF6371DDD3D0.description: Analyze data obtained from testing different materials to determine which materials have the properties that are best suited for an intended purpose.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of properties could include, strength, flexibility, hardness, texture, and absorbency.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment of quantitative measurements is limited to length.

755C69FCE86947DF87EEB0A7C6ADFE2C.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to describe and classify different kinds of materials by their observable properties.
comments: Clarification Statement: Observations could include color, texture, hardness, and flexibility. Patterns could include the similar properties that different materials share.

337311618AD54DF880BD152A86F82ED7.description: Obtain information to identify where water is found on Earth and that it can be solid or liquid.

3F78C6B086DB4776B6C229CE1D637EE9.description: Develop a model to represent the shapes and kinds of land and bodies of water in an area.
comments: Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include quantitative scaling in models.

Clarification Statement: Examples of solutions could include different designs of dikes and windbreaks to hold back wind and water, and different designs for using shrubs, grass, and trees to hold back the land.
13DB9BF0C32243A7A232CF4A5C70258A.description: Compare multiple solutions designed to slow or prevent wind or water from changing the shape of the land.

312D386AABF74B98B63D7994A397A677.description: Use information from several sources to provide evidence that Earth events can occur quickly or slowly.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of events and timescales could include volcanic explosions and earthquakes, which happen quickly and erosion of rocks, which occurs slowly.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include quantitative measurements of timescales.

FAA67D5306E749269066F36AB81ED944.description: Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
comments: Clarification Statement: Emphasis is on the diversity of living things in each of a variety of different habitats.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include specific animal and plant names in specific habitats.

3CBA8DF2C8A34854954E4C8DDFC061D5.description: Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.

983C500665F0447B90EAEAEC4EDE3A02.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to determine if plants need sunlight and water to grow.
comments: Assessment Boundary: Assessment is limited to testing one variable at a time.

CFFA3511DF754CD38CE71918E8FC1E60.description: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.

DAA833229997419195E4C7B3B17D1318.description: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem.

E2553E16237E48BDA02335A4B299AACE.description: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.

document.title: Next Generation Science Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten through Grade Twelve

1DC2548A5F5E4A5C8B1DF3C2C41158A7.description: Analyze data from tests of two objects designed to solve the same problem to compare the strengths and weaknesses of how each performs.

381E20493C3A404AA3048D2D573D07A1.description: Develop a simple sketch, drawing, or physical model to illustrate how the shape of an object helps it function as needed to solve a given problem.

D21D1B79C3C34D17916C38C00BC360C8.description: Ask questions, make observations, and gather information about a situation people want to change to define a simple problem that can be solved through the development of a new or improved object or tool.

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of structures could include umbrellas, canopies, and tents that minimize the warming effect of the sun.
C46862193C9649C788B2A947EE30EA34.description: Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area.

C01D908829734CBDB020C9B87E04E0A7.description: Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of Earth's surface could include sand, soil, rocks, and water
Assessment Boundary: Assessment of temperature is limited to relative measures such as warmer/cooler.

Clarification Statement: Examples of problems requiring a solution could include having a marble or other object move a certain distance, follow a particular path, and knock down other objects. Examples of solutions could include tools such as a ramp to increase the speed of the object and a structure that would cause an object such as a marble or ball to turn.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment does not include friction as a mechanism for change in speed.
32A87FFAF123486FBA8C6D478D8D02D4.description: Analyze data to determine if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull.

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of pushes or pulls could include a string attached to an object being pulled, a person pushing an object, a person stopping a rolling ball, and two objects colliding and pushing on each other.

Assessment Boundary: Assessment is limited to different relative strengths or different directions, but not both at the same time. Assessment does not include non-contact pushes or pulls such as those produced by magnets.
B5E41D23F6D74A479BC78E2FAB4891B5.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.

3DA8904D78AD452892BE201BE990DDCD.description: Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of human impact on the land could include cutting trees to produce paper and using resources to produce bottles. Examples of solutions could include reusing paper and recycling cans and bottles.
3B38A3AD0729440F88815ECD7FE0DAF1.description: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air, and/or other living things in the local environment.

comments: Clarification Statement: Emphasis is on local forms of severe weather.
B7E45AD9A33C4D96974E5E8ACB553250.description: Ask questions to obtain information about the purpose of weather forecasting to prepare for, and respond to, severe weather.

comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of relationships could include that deer eat buds and leaves, therefore, they usually live in forested areas; and, grasses need sunlight so they often grow in meadows. Plants, animals, and their surroundings make up a system.
124B355872A14436B1BED69BD57FC479.description: Use a model to represent the relationship between the needs of different plants or animals (including humans) and the places they live.

1EC45E50ECF947B6BED729E14693020E.description: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals (including humans) can change the environment to meet their needs.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of plants and animals changing their environment could include a squirrel digs in the ground to hide its food and tree roots can break concrete.

EEAB9A3641BC4A6F989471D50BCA9A74.description: Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of qualitative observations could include descriptions of the weather (such as sunny, cloudy, rainy, and warm); examples of quantitative observations could include numbers of sunny, windy, and rainy days in a month. Examples of patterns could include that it is usually cooler in the morning than in the afternoon and the number of sunny days versus cloudy days in different months.
Assessment Boundary: Assessment of quantitative observations limited to whole numbers and relative measures such as warmer/cooler.

A03D4E1F17C3404EAD6541AFBA65E1AA.description: Use observations to describe patterns of what plants and animals (including humans) need to survive.
comments: Clarification Statement: Examples of patterns could include that animals need to take in food but plants do not; the different kinds of food needed by different types of animals; the requirement of plants to have light; and, that all living things need water.

CD06A2B83A784E6E869AC84CCBB16391.description: From Molecules to Organisms: Structures and Processes

document.title: History-Social Science Content Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

BD324C50DFE40131FFF068A86D17958E.description: Understand how people lived in earlier times and how their lives would be different today (e.g., getting water from a well, growing food, making clothing, having fun, forming organizations, living by rules and laws).

BD320860DFE40131FFEF68A86D17958E.description: Know the triumphs in American legends and historical accounts through the stories of such people as Pocahontas, George Washing-ton, Booker T. Washington, Daniel Boone, and Benjamin Franklin.

BD31C020DFE40131FFEE68A86D17958E.description: Identify the purposes of, and the people and events honored in, commemorative holidays, including the human struggles that were the basis for the events (e.g., Thanksgiving, Independence Day, Washington's and Lincoln's Birthdays, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Memorial Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day).

BD3177A0DFE40131FFED68A86D17958E.description: Students understand that history relates to events, people, and places of other times.

BD3135D0DFE40131FFEC68A86D17958E.description: Students put events in temporal order using a calendar, placing days, weeks, and months in proper order.

BD30E9F0DFE40131FFEB68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate familiarity with the school's layout, environs, and the jobs people do there.

BD30A080DFE40131FFEA68A86D17958E.description: Construct maps and models of neighborhoods, incorporating such structures as police and fire stations, airports, banks, hospitals, supermarkets, harbors, schools, homes, places of worship, and transportation lines.

BD3054C0DFE40131FFE968A86D17958E.description: Identify traffic symbols and map symbols (e.g., those for land, water, roads, cities).

BD3011E0DFE40131FFE868A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between land and water on maps and globes and locate general areas referenced in historical legends and stories.

BD2FC6B0DFE40131FFE768A86D17958E.description: Determine the relative locations of objects using the terms near/far, left/right, and behind/in front.

BD2F8780DFE40131FFE668A86D17958E.description: Students compare and contrast the locations of people, places, and environments and describe their characteristics.

BD2F48D0DFE40131FFE568A86D17958E.description: Students match simple descriptions of work that people do and the names of related jobs at the school, in the local community, and from historical accounts.

BD2F08B0DFE40131FFE468A86D17958E.description: Students recognize national and state symbols and icons such as the national and state flags, the bald eagle, and the Statue of Liberty.

BD2EC690DFE40131FFE368A86D17958E.description: Know beliefs and related behaviors of characters in stories from times past and understand the consequences of the characters' actions.

BD2E7D70DFE40131FFE268A86D17958E.description: Learn examples of honesty, courage, determination, individual responsibility, and patriotism in American and world history from stories and folklore.

BD2E1D50DFE40131FFE168A86D17958E.description: Follow rules, such as sharing and taking turns, and know the consequences of breaking them.

BD2DCBD0DFE40131FFE068A86D17958E.description: Students understand that being a good citizen involves acting in certain ways.

BD2D8740DFE40131FFDF68A86D17958E.description: Learning and Working Now and Long Ago

BD2D47D0DFE40131FFDE68A86D17958E.description: Students conduct cost-benefit analyses of historical and current events.

BD2D0750DFE40131FFDD68A86D17958E.description: Students identify and interpret the multiple causes and effects of historical events.

BD2CC4C0DFE40131FFDC68A86D17958E.description: Students identify the human and physical characteristics of the places they are studying and explain how those features form the unique character of those places.

BD2C71F0DFE40131FFDB68A86D17958E.description: Students summarize the key events of the era they are studying and explain the historical contexts of those events.

BD2BF300DFE40131FFD968A86D17958E.description: Students distinguish fact from fiction by comparing documentary sources on historical figures and events with fictionalized characters and events.

BD2BA280DFE40131FFD868A86D17958E.description: Students pose relevant questions about events they encounter in historical documents, eyewitness accounts, oral histories, letters, diaries, artifacts, photographs, maps, artworks, and architecture.

BD2B60E0DFE40131FFD768A86D17958E.description: Students differentiate between primary and secondary sources.

BD2B1F20DFE40131FFD668A86D17958E.description: Research, Evidence, and Point of View

BD2AD3D0DFE40131FFD568A86D17958E.description: Students judge the significance of the relative location of a place (e.g., proximity to a harbor, on trade routes) and analyze how relative advantages or disadvantages can change over time.

BD2A62B0DFE40131FFD468A86D17958E.description: Students use map and globe skills to determine the absolute locations of places and interpret information available through a map's or globe's legend, scale, and symbolic representations.

BD2A0450DFE40131FFD368A86D17958E.description: Students explain how the present is connected to the past, identifying both similarities and differences between the two, and how some things change over time and some things stay the same.

BD29BAE0DFE40131FFD268A86D17958E.description: Students correctly apply terms related to time, including past, present, future, decade, century, and generation.

BD2976D0DFE40131FFD168A86D17958E.description: Students place key events and people of the historical era they are studying in a chronological sequence and within a spatial context; they interpret time lines.

BD28E780DFE40131FFCF68A86D17958E.description: Historical and Social Sciences Analysis Skills

document.title: California Common Core State Standards: Mathematics

D279D2DF521E498FAA0E6235AA04390F.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

8A24410511834B909D393DE0245C725C.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
comments: Example: express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6.
Example: locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.

BCCF01AD34A34B0D97005F482CCBCB64.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

0F6D173B12574C93982BA1FC61F11EB4.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

95E9D3E53BE74C1C9B1D1D4FAEB03972.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

52793ACD92B04F859145C7E4FD067878.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

567F40B809744000983C0341371B4770.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

6F00E8BA95A64109B863FB6DBE5502E6.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

0D68CC9CD0C44C8780C8E6A89C1BD1EA.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.

137AE179BE544F6F874828A7AB50C9FA.description: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

AD01A2F1024049E3B3EA16891444D13F.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
comments: For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape.

33D2F4160EB242729ED6112892D9A4FE.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

E1534DEE9F1C4383A3BDBA55C2B348AD.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

8B388909C2D24E4CB4B0CA2FB3FDB646.description: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

6F8285F2CA0045B19064F55C11C555CE.description: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.

36120C88E6574DCE853653F6B6B5EBD1.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

FF3AB0F6A7494077A5DE9ECEB611AE12.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

27D6EC4273EA4B99BB55E9B2ECE05443.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

0DB6E803D6694AF5A055F8A0532B1EC9.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

6082751A5FFF4EEF9DA1D40718C77C36.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.

3DD2EE70CCF94119BA1EF80F7C1614B6.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

5B99A1D0DF4E4DD4B12924855CECF797.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

646EE232A764464A9A405CB6F30DBD0E.description: A square with side length 1 unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

A7D24EAABFA9400FA784D4CAFAB4C523.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

4027DD7266CE426185EAE8456FC283C2.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

DCCCC714147543C99D33EA0BCAEA3C6E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

BFCFEDFA9A004D829070F010A355956A.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.

EC554FED7CBD429F822E456E25C7062F.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
comments: Excludes multiplicative comparison problems (problems involving notions of "times as much";
Excludes compound units such as cm³ and finding the geometric volume of a container.

9C8C24D54B3D4CEC8224C26424A482F0.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

40C5061028B14198927F1AB59C3FAF7C.description: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

985BC2C5BE3445E0976C3469D5C44908.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10—90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

9314F74097CA4E79A9E374A62818F1CD.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

2B85236AEBD3478DBEAA8FAF9E058EF0.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

FA1798E9F06041B7AB13C4CCFBDDA9FF.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
comments: A range of algorithms may be used.

48869EE79BA149378A5C8F7D6B1978AE.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

EB125ED09B1B4C178C805B7E10D11451.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
comments: For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.

1D8DA0347DBD47859291F99072ACC902.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
comments: This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).

5FB1DA8A585445D3910750A16FC908DD.description: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.

87A25D0106BB4D259F2CBD375AFF27C6.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

17519DB64D404072801C515E0159881B.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

DAA5BAAB172047D385EBC1EFC9013ED5.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)

08356712EE2E4AFD9DACE657614AC1C0.description: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.

82F7C1208CA64DBE891C3FB03766DC11.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?.

EA8D5746881449659DDF75C2FE5656CC.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

3F6C5D396E8C4C2CA1E42518611C2E81.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.

6A5063C0BFEE46ACAEE96D39C08797C9.description: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.

4B482EB8DC934A62AD0FB15A71535444.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

228344A377964FD0A6291338CA23EA30.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

55C1CDC580714D9B9F8C24F3350D4BD5.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

1152C33FA2E84BC49E27C1AD5BCC5803.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E14E861CD2524D8D8CDCD970BA7E4628.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: California English Language Development Standards

9D2A0B7C94C24520823468D417955AEA.description: Condense clauses in a variety of ways (e.g., through embedded clauses and other condensing as in, It's a plant. It's green and red. It's found in the tropical rain forest. → It's a green and red plant that's found in the tropical rain forest) to create precise and detailed sentences independently.

3A08C8356B004FD9A3FB16757379DB40.description: Condense clauses in a growing number of ways (e.g., through embedded clauses as in, It's a plant. It's found in the rain forest. → It's a green and red plant that's found in the rain forest) to create precise and detailed sentences with increasing independence.

D4CE14C0E94B420DA39EED0FFCE3C810.description: Condense clauses in simple ways (e.g., changing: It's green. It's red. → It's green and red) to create precise and detailed sentences in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

8A4997FD442842F88E5DF96A38CA190E.description: Combine clauses in a wide variety of ways (e.g., rearranging complete, simple-to-form compound sentences) to make connections between and to join ideas (e.g., The boy was hungry. The boy ate a sandwich. → The boy was hungry so he ate a sandwich) independently.

18D84EE737524CFCAD80708D9F349681.description: Combine clauses in an increasing variety of ways to make connections between and to join ideas, for example, to express cause/effect (e.g., She jumped because the dog barked) with increasing independence.

EC2A60965B3A4489AA6CA0C2966E2E15.description: Combine clauses in a few basic ways to make connections between and to join ideas (e.g., creating compound sentences using and, but, so) in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

B454D44E311B48EF86CE6387B9C9086B.description: Expand sentences with a variety of adverbials (e.g., adverbs, adverb phrases, prepositional phrases) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) independently.

B78225B64D9D4CA097DB107A4717F1DA.description: Expand sentences with a growing number of adverbials (e.g., adverbs, prepositional phrases) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) about a familiar or new activity or process with increasing independence.

14ECFFC22C294025A9D8D2A5CF435FAD.description: Expand sentences with frequently used adverbials (e.g., prepositional phrases, such as at school, with my friend) to provide details (e.g., time, manner, place, cause) about a familiar activity or process in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

5F86AE6CA1D1415D87231AA4DC171163.description: Expand noun phrases in a variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative adjectives to nouns) in order to enrich the meaning of phrases/sentences and to add details about ideas, people, things, and the like, independently.

2EBF6BB6BF884A2F9E4CEDCDE2E30D62.description: Expand noun phrases in a growing number of ways (e.g., adding a newly learned adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and to add details about ideas, people, things, and the like, with increasing independence.

0D8D851930AA45CAB8D92ED6632B6F27.description: Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a familiar adjective to describe a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and to add details about ideas, people, things, and the like, in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

A8125351D2ED43749F509E7DEF60216E.description: Use a wide variety of verb tenses appropriate to the text type and discipline to convey time (e.g., simple present tense for a science description, simple future to predict) independently.

1E04CD786D8A407D832C19F3C3A7B8E2.description: Use a variety of verb types (e.g., doing, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling) independently.

75999ADD1DF44191A616638B83E50847.description: Use a growing number of verb tenses appropriate to the text type and discipline to convey time (e.g., simple past tense for retelling, simple present for a science description) with increasing independence.

FA996D0B708C40FA873362E65E58560D.description: Use a growing number of verb types (e.g., doing, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling) with increasing independence.

706D77F494E447C9B7EA165DC56814FD.description: Use simple verb tenses appropriate to the text type and discipline to convey time (e.g., simple past tense for recounting an experience) in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

8556F3E9C686493CA4CC4D7BD6ABA1B4.description: Use frequently used verbs (e.g., walk, run) and verb types (e.g., doing, saying, being/having, thinking/feeling) in shared language activities guided by the teacher and sometimes independently.

E947E84A9B8540BEA69159A88357B49A.description: Apply understanding of how ideas, events, or reasons are linked throughout a text using a variety of connecting words or phrases (e.g., for example, after that, suddenly) to comprehending and writing texts independently.

A7E9D44CA3E044DC8197D445B454D018.description: Apply understanding of how ideas, events, or reasons are linked throughout a text using a growing number of connecting words or phrases (e.g., after a long time, first/next) to comprehending texts and writing texts with increasing independence.

CA3174E2DDE44441A0FFBF01BDE15104.description: Apply basic understanding of how ideas, events, or reasons are linked throughout a text using more everyday connecting words or phrases (e.g., today, then) to comprehending and composing texts in shared language activities guided by the teacher, with peers, and sometimes independently.

FF929B932C474546BD7AFDDD71337537.description: Apply understanding of how different text types are organized predictably to express ideas (e.g., a narrative versus an informative/explanatory text versus an opinion text) to comprehending and writing texts independently.

D0DDBA1DE0D748A7AFA69C908DD8378E.description: Apply understanding of how different text types are organized to express ideas (e.g., how a story is organized sequentially with predictable stages versus how an information report is organized by topic and details) to comprehending texts and composing texts with increasing independence.

994BD720A708430C8FF8BAF9F6F0ACD1.description: Apply understanding of how different text types are organized to express ideas (e.g., how a story is organized sequentially) to comprehending and composing texts in shared language activities guided by the teacher, with peers, and sometimes independently.

269BE880261747B1AA7CA5708FC198FF.description: Use a wide variety of general academic and domain-specific words, synonyms, antonyms, and non-literal language (e.g., He was as quick as a cricket) to create an effect, precision, and shades of meaning while speaking and writing.

4414DD248AB141C7856D14343E615957.description: Retell texts and recount experiences using increasingly detailed complete sentences and key words.

3FD5DD33DE304DB2A7196B9F8F0D63F2.description: Use a growing number of general academic and domain-specific words in order to add detail, create an effect (e.g., using the word suddenly to signal a change), or create shades of meaning (e.g., scurry versus dash) while speaking and writing.

0AF77C96EF9C404289D66F75AB8325AA.description: Retell texts and recount experiences using complete sentences and key words.

FF6AA705D7464F95B6286BB792DB3A51.description: Use a select number of general academic and domain-specific words to add detail (e.g., adding the word generous to describe a character, using the word lava to explain volcanic eruptions) while speaking and writing.

41ECCED66FB3439ABBB237D4741D9487.description: Retell texts and recount experiences by using key words.

24B8D4A5B8614C38AE4751B93679D85C.description: Selecting and applying varied and precise vocabulary and language structures to effectively convey ideas

B790268A5797493E8A9631A03D2D5EA0.description: Support opinions or persuade others by providing good reasons and detailed textual evidence (e.g., specific events or graphics from text) or relevant background knowledge about the content.

C15FC22025014DA39FDCCCBD60B40552.description: Support opinions by providing good reasons and increasingly detailed textual evidence (e.g., providing examples from the text) or relevant background knowledge about the content.

DDB3486933C84C6E94CCCC4C5058B9F4.description: Support opinions by providing good reasons and some textual evidence or relevant background knowledge (e.g., referring to textual evidence or knowledge of content).

A7B96B4C1BD347BE8E1870EA6AA6330E.description: Supporting own opinions and evaluating others' opinions in speaking and writing

C9201C4132EA44F6AC2AF37D4BC95492.description: Write longer literary texts (e.g., a story) and informational texts (e.g., an explanatory text explaining how a volcano erupts) collaboratively with an adult (e.g., joint construction), with peers and independently.

E9497ADA31AD451A83645950A2726351.description: Write short literary texts (e.g., a story) and informational texts (e.g., an explanatory text explaining how a volcano erupts) collaboratively with an adult (e.g., joint construction of texts), with peers, and with increasing independence.

DEF9F9DCABAF4B63ADC9FE1F2086AFA1.description: Write very short literary texts (e.g., story) and informational texts (e.g., a description of a volcano) using familiar vocabulary collaboratively with an adult (e.g., joint construction of texts), with peers, and sometimes independently.

28ADBD50CDD14492AD0FCC93C68D5FBE.description: Writing literary and informational texts to present, describe, and explain ideas and information, using appropriate technology

B799D1E2A3854AA6813B78CD1C9E43CF.description: Plan and deliver longer oral presentations on a variety of topics and content areas (e.g., retelling a story, recounting a science experiment, describing how to solve a mathematics problem).

6DA242651C1C45BCAEFD61F85C4E1ADE.description: Plan and deliver brief oral presentations on a variety of topics (e.g., retelling a story, describing an animal).

1781824966B542EDBE840299CC4AC756.description: Plan and deliver very brief oral presentations (e.g., recounting an experience, retelling a story, describing a picture).

41AFBCAB29CA4543B708E4DAD803E5E5.description: Expressing information and ideas in formal oral presentations on academic topics

338C5327B8284FE18978FBD4E0C3DDD7.description: Productive (creation of oral presentations and written texts)

9C8053C0A8DB4E5994398A388EC529BC.description: Distinguish how multiple different words with similar meaning (e.g., pleased versus happy versus ecstatic, heard or knew versus believed) produce shades of meaning and different effects on the audience.

53B5981C03E649CC9771A161BC98F7B4.description: Distinguish how two different words with similar meaning (e.g., describing a character as happy versus ecstatic) produce shades of meaning and different effects on the audience.

3F67E006E8E04B269CB39597A229E8A6.description: Distinguish how two different frequently used words (e.g., describing a character as happy versus angry) produce a different effect on the audience.

303BF8D8A4F640208D879A30B6D44C44.description: Analyzing how writers and speakers use vocabulary and other language resources for specific purposes (to explain, persuade, entertain, etc.) depending on modality, text type, purpose, audience, topic, and content area

3487DEDA4C674B92BCED687D88DC7D6E.description: Describe how well writers or speakers use specific language resources to support an opinion or present an idea (e.g., whether the vocabulary used to present evidence is strong enough), with light support.

AE8366B945CE42179DB8F4B2AE9459DD.description: Describe the language writers or speakers use to present or support an idea (e.g., the author's choice of vocabulary or phrasing to portray characters, places, or real people), with prompting and moderate support.

02DB367C51AE4742B0A9D67AAF3310FE.description: Describe the language writers or speakers use to present an idea (e.g., the words and phrases used to describe a character), with prompting and substantial support.

DC03D848B21A44F5AB1C38E70562CC07.description: Evaluating how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and opinions with details or reasons depending on modality, text type, purpose, audience, topic, and content area

BA51049DB9AC4E2BA1B21AA5E2C013AE.description: Describe ideas, phenomena (e.g., erosion), and text elements (e.g., central message, character traits) using key details based on understanding of a variety of grade-level texts and viewing of multimedia, with light support.

03DAD0C7B8C1465EA9D7049A258490E7.description: Describe ideas, phenomena (e.g., how earthworms eat), and text elements (e.g., setting, events) in greater detail based on understanding of a variety of grade-level texts and viewing of multimedia, with moderate support.

85D8AE33BFB345438B02E3530CCA85DF.description: Describe ideas, phenomena (e.g., plant life cycle), and text elements (e.g., main idea, characters, events) based on understanding of a select set of grade-level texts and viewing of multimedia, with substantial support.

653566C5D2B148389909E1C2C6849568.description: Reading closely literary and informational texts and viewing multimedia to determine how meaning is conveyed explicitly and implicitly through language

4DB9E745C81F4CB5BF9CC210CF015859.description: Demonstrate active listening to read-alouds and oral presentations by asking and answering detailed questions, with minimal prompting and light support.

212683359BD24AB5A98CC8A44D872053.description: Demonstrate active listening to read-alouds and oral presentations by asking and answering detailed questions, with oral sentence frames and occasional prompting and support.

A052CAAF186E485BB05B46A2367B1E7B.description: Demonstrate active listening to read-alouds and oral presentations by asking and answering basic questions, with oral sentence frames and substantial prompting and support.

CE581797DC8145948BD17D62C758E45F.description: Listening actively to spoken English in a range of social and academic contexts

6487C36D8A55494CBC15C3364ACE3779.description: Interpretive (comprehension and analysis of written and spoken texts)

40C86FF93FC244A28208E7C9049792D5.description: Adjust language choices according to purpose (e.g., persuading, entertaining), task, and audience (e.g., peer-to-peer versus peer-to-teacher), with light support from peers or adults.

4AB729FF0E5544C48126E4A827FD4B0F.description: Adjust language choices (e.g., vocabulary, use of dialogue, and so on) according to purpose (e.g., persuading, entertaining), task, and audience (e.g., peers versus adults), with moderate support from peers or adults.

9307B14CD2CE4E4EB3CC419BBA1E6116.description: Recognize that language choices (e.g., vocabulary) vary according to social setting (e.g., playground versus classroom), with substantial support from peers or adults.

61CFACBCEB724E018101D5036016FE3A.description: Adapting language choices to various contexts (based on task, purpose, audience, and text type)

BF45786762334E1FACBD2E443AF73125.description: Offer opinions and negotiate with others in conversations using a variety of learned phrases (e.g., That's a good idea, but X), as well as open responses, in order to gain and/or hold the floor, provide counterarguments, elaborate on an idea, and the like.

580D9FB4BA474FD6AEEC58AEB9511E27.description: Offer opinions and negotiate with others in conversations using an expanded set of learned phrases (e.g., I agree with X, but X.), as well as open responses, in order to gain and/or hold the floor, provide counterarguments, and the like.

CC9EF415801A46CD89BD47FEC397D991.description: Offer opinions and negotiate with others in conversations using learned phrases (e.g., I think X.), as well as open responses, in order to gain and/or hold the floor.

DF8D58B306C34E85B1BF73E19426F661.description: Offering and supporting opinions and negotiating with others in communicative exchanges

6C677358F68A49208B0C45330DDBFCF9.description: Collaborate with peers on joint writing projects of a variety of longer informational and literary texts, using technology where appropriate for publishing, graphics, and the like.

CDED2995BE954525A50E28609E3AC59E.description: Collaborate with peers on joint writing projects of longer informational and literary texts, using technology where appropriate for publishing, graphics, and the like.

41BAEE0A63DF47F4AC0731D0335B0871.description: Collaborate with peers on joint writing projects of short informational and literary texts, using technology where appropriate for publishing, graphics, and the like.

4DD6370746F4468F9393D8CC949FF809.description: Interacting with others in written English in various communicative forms (print, communicative technology, and multimedia)

B4217A93B5E94AB4BD214AABD0884987.description: Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions, including sustained dialogue, by listening attentively, following turn-taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding pertinent information, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.

0712964465CE418E9EDF9DCBA923BEDB.description: Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions, including sustained dialogue, by listening attentively, following turn-taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, and adding relevant information.

61F4AE57FDE743A4BE8FBC7B2FDF7DFB.description: Contribute to conversations and express ideas by asking and answering yes-no and wh- questions and responding using gestures, words, and learned phrases.

A6D62B891A4B4C6387E3EDBA636C7E25.description: Exchanging information and ideas with others through oral collaborative conversations on a range of social and academic topics

document.title: History-Social Science Content Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

BD70D2A0DFE40131006668A86D17958E.description: Discuss the relationship of students' "work" in school and their personal human capital.

BD7087D0DFE40131006568A86D17958E.description: Understand that individual economic choices involve trade-offs and the evaluation of benefits and costs.

BD702E40DFE40131006468A86D17958E.description: Understand that some goods are made locally, some elsewhere in the United States, and some abroad.

BD6FDD70DFE40131006368A86D17958E.description: Describe the ways in which local producers have used and are using natural resources, human resources, and capital resources to produce goods and services in the past and the present.

BD6F98B0DFE40131006268A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate basic economic reasoning skills and an understanding of the economy of the local region.

BD6F52C0DFE40131006168A86D17958E.description: Describe the lives of American heroes who took risks to secure our freedoms (e.g., Anne Hutchinson, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, Martin Luther King, Jr.).

BD6F0CD0DFE40131006068A86D17958E.description: Describe the ways in which California, the other states, and sovereign American Indian tribes contribute to the making of our nation and participate in the federal system of government.

BD6ECA40DFE40131005F68A86D17958E.description: Understand the three branches of government, with an emphasis on local government.

BD6E77F0DFE40131005E68A86D17958E.description: Know the histories of important local and national landmarks, symbols, and essential documents that create a sense of community among citizens and exemplify cherished ideals (e.g., the U.S. flag, the bald eagle, the Statue of Liberty, the U.S. Constitution, the Declaration of Independence, the U.S. Capitol).

BD6E1E20DFE40131005D68A86D17958E.description: Discuss the importance of public virtue and the role of citizens, including how to participate in a classroom, in the community, and in civic life.

BD6DB390DFE40131005C68A86D17958E.description: Determine the reasons for rules, laws, and the U.S. Constitution; the role of citizenship in the promotion of rules and laws; and the consequences for people who violate rules and laws.

BD6D6A30DFE40131005B68A86D17958E.description: Students understand the role of rules and laws in our daily lives and the basic structure of the U.S. government.

BD6D2D00DFE40131005A68A86D17958E.description: Trace why their community was established, how individuals and families contributed to its founding and development, and how the community has changed over time, drawing on maps, photographs, oral histories, letters, newspapers, and other primary sources.

BD6CEDC0DFE40131005968A86D17958E.description: Describe the economies established by settlers and their influence on the present-day economy, with emphasis on the importance of private property and entrepreneurship.

BD6CAA40DFE40131005868A86D17958E.description: Research the explorers who visited here, the newcomers who settled here, and the people who continue to come to the region, including their cultural and religious traditions and contributions.

BD6C5EF0DFE40131005768A86D17958E.description: Students draw from historical and community resources to organize the sequence of local historical events and describe how each period of settlement left its mark on the land.

BD6C1E50DFE40131005668A86D17958E.description: Discuss the interaction of new settlers with the already established Indians of the region.

BD6BDD10DFE40131005568A86D17958E.description: Describe the economy and systems of government, particularly those with tribal constitutions, and their relationship to federal and state governments.

BD6B9B20DFE40131005468A86D17958E.description: Discuss the ways in which physical geography, including climate, influenced how the local Indian nations adapted to their natural environment (e.g., how they obtained food, clothing, tools).

BD6B57E0DFE40131005368A86D17958E.description: Describe national identities, religious beliefs, customs, and various folklore traditions.

BD6B09B0DFE40131005268A86D17958E.description: Students describe the American Indian nations in their local region long ago and in the recent past.

BD6AC150DFE40131005168A86D17958E.description: Trace the ways in which people have used the resources of the local region and modified the physical environment (e.g., a dam constructed upstream changed a river or coastline).

BD6A6C10DFE40131005068A86D17958E.description: Identify geographical features in their local region (e.g., deserts, mountains, valleys, hills, coastal areas, oceans, lakes).

BD6A2D00DFE40131004F68A86D17958E.description: Students describe the physical and human geography and use maps, tables, graphs, photographs, and charts to organize information about people, places, and environments in a spatial context.

BD69B080DFE40131004D68A86D17958E.description: Students conduct cost-benefit analyses of historical and current events.

BD6971F0DFE40131004C68A86D17958E.description: Students identify and interpret the multiple causes and effects of historical events.

BD692F70DFE40131004B68A86D17958E.description: Students identify the human and physical characteristics of the places they are studying and explain how those features form the unique character of those places.

BD68EA00DFE40131004A68A86D17958E.description: Students summarize the key events of the era they are studying and explain the historical contexts of those events.

BD685200DFE40131004868A86D17958E.description: Students distinguish fact from fiction by comparing documentary sources on historical figures and events with fictionalized characters and events.

BD680AF0DFE40131004768A86D17958E.description: Students pose relevant questions about events they encounter in historical documents, eyewitness accounts, oral histories, letters, diaries, artifacts, photographs, maps, artworks, and architecture.

BD67CB20DFE40131004668A86D17958E.description: Students differentiate between primary and secondary sources.

BD6787B0DFE40131004568A86D17958E.description: Research, Evidence, and Point of View

BD673040DFE40131004468A86D17958E.description: Students judge the significance of the relative location of a place (e.g., proximity to a harbor, on trade routes) and analyze how relative advantages or disadvantages can change over time.

BD66E4B0DFE40131004368A86D17958E.description: Students use map and globe skills to determine the absolute locations of places and interpret information available through a map's or globe's legend, scale, and symbolic representations.

BD669DD0DFE40131004268A86D17958E.description: Students explain how the present is connected to the past, identifying both similarities and differences between the two, and how some things change over time and some things stay the same.

BD665A30DFE40131004168A86D17958E.description: Students correctly apply terms related to time, including past, present, future, decade, century, and generation.

BD6616A0DFE40131004068A86D17958E.description: Students place key events and people of the historical era they are studying in a chronological sequence and within a spatial context; they interpret time lines.

BD658430DFE40131003E68A86D17958E.description: Historical and Social Sciences Analysis Skills

document.title: California Common Core State Standards: English Language Arts and Literacy
