and how they appear to move and
change.

468491C9553E4688AA5EDC2AFF4FBD82.description:
Demonstrate increased ability
to investigate and compare charac­ teristics (size, weight, shape, color, texture) of earth materials such as sand, rocks, soil, water, and air.

E3D77203C5794607AB0578334F468CEA.description:
Investigate characteristics (size, weight, shape, color, texture) of earth materials such as sand, rocks, soil,
water, and air.

93A663BD32914C25B2893CC7F61A5305.description: Properties and Characteristics of Earth Materials and Objects

F2F2DB22E3304927AB8823B2A158F1E4.description:
Develop a greater understanding
of the basic needs of humans, animals, and plants (e.g., food, water, sunshine, shelter).

9640FF12AA9E477B8C343A6602129EF4.description: Observe and explore growth in hu­mans, animals, and plants and dem­onstrate an increased understanding that living things change as they grow and go through transformations relat­ed to the life cycle (for example, from a caterpillar to butter y).

EE2E9612504140068FBBCD51FE7D75FF.description: Recognize that animals and plants require care and begin to associate feeding and watering with the growth of humans, animals, and plants.

903DB26BFDA94F228565B94D823D1EAC.description: Observe and explore growth and changes in humans, animals, and plants and demonstrate an under­ standing that living things change over time in size and in other capaci­ties as they grow.

7366E1CE0A1C4E0B99C4DAB1B0B63E13.description:
Indicate knowledge of the difference between animate and inanimate objects, providing greater detail, and recognize that only animals and plants undergo biological processes such as growth, illness, healing,
and dying.

618D117C9A9848F4A36FD718E0DDBE23.description: Recognize that living things have habitats in different environments suited to their unique needs.

871A8E31E851438E93A19DE9243E48E6.description: Indicate greater knowledge of body parts and processes (e.g., eating, sleeping, breathing, walking) in humans and other animals.

BD989DF2E3C34E59A9B4166DF35AE242.description: Identify characteristics of a greater variety of animals and plants and demonstrate an increased ability to categorize them.

F9A183A6BC3443B68B40BA4F4B8FD705.description:
Indicate knowledge of the difference between animate objects (animals, people) and inanimate objects. For example, expect animate objects
to initiate movement and to have different insides than inanimate objects.

D6DB3017ACD94AA9A36C582C417B30A4.description: Identify the habitats of people and familiar animals and plants in the environment and begin to realize that living things have habitats in different environments.

78AAF807D2434DAA900671602BA945CF.description: Begin to indicate knowledge of body parts and processes (e.g., eating, sleeping, breathing, walking) in humans and other animals.

9FF64D3389454A1CA2F3A978E8F00A59.description: Identify characteristics of a variety of animals and plants, including appearance (inside and outside) and behavior, and begin to categorize them.

E05FB9A36CD845D1A593C09E07AF20C3.description: Properties and Characteristics of Living Things

609673E3C4164091B3A802895AFF4F67.description:
Demonstrate an increased ability
to observe and describe in greater detail the motion of objects (in terms of speed, direction, the ways things move), and to explore the effect of own actions on the motion of objects, including changes in speed and direction.

A4E6FEF708C44EF2AF41766B036789EB.description: Demonstrate an increased aware­ ness that objects and materials can change in various ways. Explore and describe in greater detail changes in objects and materials (rearrangement of parts; change in color, shape, texture, form, and temperature).

112C79EB778C404CA7D8A1ABD500BFAF.description: Observe and describe the motion of objects (in terms of speed, direction, the ways things move), and explore the effect of own actions (e.g., pushing pulling, rolling, dropping) on making objects move.

B865976200D84335AD2333F7BEFBF8C1.description: Demonstrate awareness that objects and materials can change; explore and describe changes in objects and materials (rearrangement of parts; change in color, shape, texture, temperature).

E5728BEBA0D54366BE16217C071DFF95.description: Changes in Nonliving Objects and Materials

32F8481E7A85468F92A61B95C3689421.description:
Demonstrate increased ability to observe, investigate, and describe in greater detail the characteristics and physical properties of objects and
of solid and non-solid materials (size, weight, shape, color, texture, and sound).

448FA3E1DA2C401996D7C06B396B09FF.description: Observe, investigate, and identify the characteristics and physical properties of objects and of solid and non-solid materials (size, weight, shape, color, texture, and sound).

CB8F48DFB4504F3BB3BBA5389BF2A9FF.description: Properties and Characteristics of Nonliving Objects and Materials

B75207D62A534AED87CA0A600B049A1B.description: Share findings and explanations, which may be correct or incorrect, more spontaneously and with greater detail.

292FEC5633E644559CE26ED8580A2965.description: Record information more regularly and in greater detail in various ways, with adult assistance, including pictures, words (dictated to adults), charts, journals, models, photos, or by tallying and graphing information

5E1CE3456B244679885EB44662283D07.description:
Share findings and explanations, 2.2 which may be correct or incorrect,
with or without adult prompting.

946915078B0E4EDAA8FB31B7F21FC602.description:
Record observations or findings in 2.1
various ways, with adult assistance,
including pictures, words (dictated to
adults), charts, journals, models, and
photos.

EBBD3102F7534BCCB8E4C80FEA62373D.description: Demonstrate an increased ability to make inferences and form generalizations based on evidence.

B2F79D3FE0194DD3BFF22D19E70CAA94.description: Demonstrate an increased ability to make predictions and check them (e.g., may make more complex predictions, offer ways to test predictions, and discuss why predictions were correct or incorrect).

F4FC72149E2D45DFAE8DA32F53D86F82.description: Compare and contrast objects and events and describe similarities and differences in greater detail.

6DF01E41BBC042659AF0397E8B4F1CA3.description: Identify and use a greater variety of observation and measurement tools. May spontaneously use an appropriate tool, though may still need adult support.

06628C8CFB9F48579ECD1F87B60A6404.description: Observe objects and events in the environment and describe them in greater detail.

55D64BA4A3D142CDBAD5E110CBD9F568.description: Demonstrate curiosity and an increased ability to raise questions about objects and events in their environment.

968AD2B5301A4D25B3A547A69E37F616.description: Make inferences and form generaliza­tions based on evidence.

FC2768142A31405C91D501BC26DD611A.description: Make predictions and check them, with adult support, through concrete experiences.

4106B48671D64633BC8A421CA517246E.description: Compare and contrast objects and events and begin to describe similarities and differences.

F766E8CC259E4C878A54DDF6C3CE5715.description: Begin to identify and use, with adult support, some observation and measurement tools.

34324A6EC7684BB1940841CE621972F8.description: Observe1 objects and events in the environment and describe them.

70DA8226251B43329DD4FE6CA8D2069E.description:
Demonstrate curiosity and raise simple questions about objects and
events in their environment.

document.title: California Preschool Foundations Volume 3

CEDFC3F98BDC4C42A5696A7E40E049D6.description: Understand more complex economic concepts (e.g., bartering; more money is needed for things of greater value; if more people want something, more will be sold).

CA92BAC186F44CC2A3F4DA5476ED87F0.description: Understand ownership, limited supply, what stores do, give-­and­-take, and payment of money to sellers. Show interest in money and its function, but still figuring out the relative value of coins.

28A1C59A08674F5F8ADCD31B7D0E5C3B.description: Create their own drawings, maps, and models; are more skilled at using globes, maps, and map symbols; and use maps for basic problem solving (such as locating objects) with adult guidance.

A7791E57E2D54141981CA8ACF3929B52.description: Can use drawings, globes, and maps to refer to the physical world, although often unclear on the use of map symbols.

4B6FCF23FB574895B01A32ACF67364A4.description: Understanding the Physical World Through Drawings and Maps

D64FE9CE460342189AFC1BCA7C56CAB6.description: Show an interest in a wider range of natural phenomena, including those not directly experienced (such as snow for a child living in Southern California), and are more concerned about caring for the natural world and the positive and negative impacts of people on the natural world (e.g., recycling, putting trash in trash cans).

0B89BB055F374057BA8597DA329145FB.description: Show an interest in nature (including animals, plants, and weather) especially as children have direct experience with them. Begin to understand human interactions with the environment (such as pollution in a lake or stream) and the importance of taking care of plants and animals.

2E92A6E55E454593833E7225C06BB197.description:
Comprehend larger familiar loca­tions, such as the characteristics of their community and region (including hills and streams, weather, common activities) and the distances between familiar locations (such as between home and school), and compare
their home community with those of others.

33258942AFE243ADA1DED85E61AC3CC6.description: Identify the characteristics of familiar locations such as home and school, describe objects and activities as­sociated with each, recognize the routes between them, and begin using simple directional language (with various degrees of accuracy).

21E8467277FA42FEA7F83DE45019671A.description: Develop an interest in family history (e.g., when family members were children) as well as events of “long ago,” and begin to understand when these events occurred in relation to each other.

25476279EAF54D788C57DC43BA48AF4B.description: Easily distinguish older family members from younger ones (and other people) and events in the recent past from those that happened “long ago,” although do not readily sequence historical events on a timeline.

EFBB6C2B6D2F4E518C7FB297A2AAE992.description: Historical Changes in People and the World

8D6D433857C7440689C93578E515C4BB.description: Compare current abilities with skills at a younger age and share more detailed autobiographical stories about recent experiences.

5E44224D540F41689F619B139BE21842.description: Proudly display developing skills to attract adult attention and share simple accounts about recent experiences.

CF63F476694346F793F361D4C0D9AD71.description: Distinguish when future events will happen, plan for them, and make choices (with adult assistance) that anticipate future needs.

855BE32FC45E4AE1A2CAB1A48A5D5CEB.description: Anticipate events in familiar situations in the near future, with adult assistance.

F43A5D31BB2C438895C5FAD81E13C435.description: Show improving ability to relate past events to other past events and current experiences, although adult assistance continues to be important.

793DA07D02A2455BBC36239A4FE5BD02.description: Recall past experiences easily and enjoy hearing stories about the past, but require adult help to determine when past events occurred in relation to each other and to connect them with current experience.

DCC687F865B748D28C8AD2E69548A6F1.description: More capable of negotiating, compromising, and finding cooperative means of resolving conflict with peers or adults, although verbal aggression may also result.

AFE43BAE1C3E4C5FA095E9304A8C2FD6.description:
Can use simple bargaining strategies and seek adult assistance when in
conflict with other children or adults, although frustration, distress, or aggression also occurs.

87224B81A16C40909EA00418077B1CD0.description: Pay attention to others’ feelings, more likely to provide assistance, and try to coordinate personal desires with those of other children in mutually satisfactory ways. Actively support rules that protect fairness to others.

38317610926943D2BC2DFBABDD6A4089.description: Respond to the feelings and needs of others with simple forms of assistance, sharing, and turn-taking. Understand the importance of rules that protect fairness and maintain order.

FB31941B98A147DEB162411D08CD7D62.description: Fairness and Respect for Other People

F4652E53F5814497A74E67DA1082D62E.description: Exhibit responsible conduct more reliably as children develop self­ esteem (and adult approval) from being responsible group members. May also manage others’ behavior to ensure that others also  t in with group expectations.

2A4D0ABB01FF4EF2B3B4E1D6DDA9AFE1.description: Strive to cooperate with group expectations to maintain adult approval and get along with others. Self­-control is inconsistent, however, especially when children are frus­trated or upset.

9F9B8FC877B44C318C8F627CDD2D44BB.description: Become involved as responsible participants in group activities, with growing understanding of the importance of considering others’ opinions, group decision making, and respect for majority rules and the views of group members who disagree with the majority.

F1FABE6A98B942BCA3DCC8851BE40FA5.description: Identify as members of a group, participate willingly in group activities, and begin to understand and accept responsibility as group members, although assistance is required in coordinating personal interests with those of others.

759233F49ADF43EFA64768BCFB7A27A5.description:
Exhibit more sophisticated understanding of a broader variety of adult roles and occupations, but uncertain how work relates
to income.

625B39140D604BCEAA75AF9DF0225426.description: Play familiar adult social roles and occupations (such as parent, teacher, and doctor) consistent with their developing knowledge of these roles.

FE4FF0E0245D47C283F85E6187653D80.description: Understand the mutual responsibilities of relationships; take initiative in developing relationships that are mutual, cooperative, and exclusive.

8D5F22C9896F4CD39DF554CCE9AA5BF2.description: Interact comfortably with many peers and adults; actively contribute to creating and maintaining relation­ships with a few significant adults and peers.

BADF700FF79C40F99909DA655E3B0914.description: Manifest stronger cultural, ethnic, and racial identity and greater familiarity with relevant language, traditions, and other practices. Show more interest in human diversity, but strongly favor characteristics of their own group.

3949439923504E6FB6EC41C28CEA05E1.description: Exhibit developing cultural, ethnic, and racial identity and understand relevant language and cultural practices. Display curiosity about diversity in human characteristics and practices, but prefer those of their own group.

document.title: California Preschool Foundations Volume 1

DCE36D61EDAA4B8CB2E18DE469650864.description: Identify and apply a variety of math­ematical strategies to solve problems in their environment.

62A36412DE444E91BB03A3AA52C3B30C.description: Children expand the use of mathematical thinking to solve problems that arise in their everyday environment.

A2D7801B7FD14632B6D570DBB467F344.description: Begin to apply simple mathematical strategies to solve problems in their environment.

81CDAFCE98754BA4AC95B43B540E4874.description: Children use mathematical thinking to solve problems that arise in their everyday environment.

9DE5FAE58D7B411FB563270DF3489843.description: Identify positions of objects and people in space, including in/on/ under, up/down, inside/outside, beside/between, and in front/behind.

A2B9EAE6D0B44E3C88D7E2EEB6BDA9DC.description: Children expand their understanding of positions in space.

0A98EAFB94B64E0F91BD2B3B7DEA8F6D.description: Combine different shapes to create a picture or design.

491152EF91C64B7190F6EF79206D4968.description: Identify, describe, and construct a variety of different shapes, including variations of a circle, triangle, rect­ angle, square, and other shapes.

9373FF378A6A40D99DC2D2CC052C0B12.description: Children identify and use a variety of shapes in their everyday environment.

7CECF082351B48BEA648BF345EB604C2.description: Identify positions of objects and people in space, such as in/on/ under, up/down, and inside/outside.

56DB611E9F83462BA828E840DEA4CB35.description: Children begin to understand positions in space.

9A35FD47C43C4761BC564492E9183C16.description:
Use individual shapes to represent different elements of a picture
or design.

D4184B2045A64372ACA77389BE06E717.description: Identify simple two-dimensional shapes, such as a circle and square.

681F8C368E5E4C70B1CD51E0748579AE.description: Children begin to identify and use common shapes in their everyday environment.

9B50178A025A48168FC172A5AA4B6947.description: Measure length using multiple duplicates of the same-size concrete units laid end to end.

35B06A8F1EB6446A8D679D1CDCF0E0FF.description: Order four or more objects by size.

5D0C0457E2CE443EA4D8C46DC47E7D26.description:
Compare two objects by length, weight, or capacity directly
(e.g., putting objects side by side) or indirectly (e.g., using a third object).

12CE5DF83CC04AC7BC9B12440FC8DE76.description: Children expand their understanding of comparing, ordering, and measuring objects.

E677D32F59BF41D49F559B78284D0696.description: Demonstrate awareness that objects can be compared by length, weight, or capacity, by noting gross differences, using words such as bigger, longer, heavier, or taller, or by placing objects side by side to compare length.

203CA7DF6A824510A4329DB9075B389F.description: Children begin to compare and order objects.

C29940EF942E49B9B1A3B77F771C10FC.description: Begin to extend and create simple repeating patterns.

F865DEBE39484DC6BBEF2E9BDFB35991.description: Recognize and duplicate simple repeating patterns.

50EFF08DB01D4D21B8CE1F32344F4103.description: Children expand their understanding of simple, repeating patterns.

F3699C9192894E48A4B29E3B6C7A89BA.description: Sort and classify objects by one or more attributes, into two or more groups, with increasing accuracy (e.g., may sort  rst by one attribute and then by another attribute).

FBA25C679C454E44A83B21941962CEAE.description:
Children expand their understanding of sorting
and classifying objects in their everyday environment.

67B83D01BA7546838AFDA59BD10A6DDA.description: Attempt to create a simple repeating pattern or participate in making one.

112E48CB3E554A01A6131BAE3871B29E.description: Begin to identify or recognize a simple repeating pattern.

7AACDA2D08024CD399A9EFBBF088DDD5.description: Children begin to recognize simple, repeating patterns.

3BA60D04073341018ED60904F57991CC.description: Sort and classify objects by one attribute into two or more groups, with increasing accuracy.

D861AAED4E4B4DA78F506AF3F7802D74.description:
Children begin to sort
and classify objects in their everyday environment.

005610C7D908460380A593E53EF6DDD2.description: Solve simple addition and subtrac­ tion problems with a small number of objects (sums up to 10), usually by counting.

1876881F9F664273A1B764B5CAF2C94C.description: Understand that putting two groups of objects together will make a bigger group and that a group of objects can be taken apart into smaller groups.

EFE89A8FBFF746F9938DDB3B9F6C1103.description: Understand that adding one or taking away one changes the number in a small group of objects by exactly one.

1678198D4A014D0EB7A7283B1DAA087C.description: Compare, by counting or matching, two groups of up to  ve objects and communicate, “more,” “same as,” or “fewer” (or “less”).

501D0472DEAA48E29D41F6C595A7E819.description: Children expand their under­ standing of number relation­ ships and operations in their everyday environment.

B1A445C40AE44E879BF38FB9BFBAC626.description: Understand, when counting, that the number name of the last object counted represents the total number of objects in the group (i.e., cardinality).

D708353CB1074F08A3C4B3C7DBA64FF1.description:
Count up to ten objects, using one-to-one correspondence
(one object for each number word) with increasing accuracy.

8B48701CCCC54658B683CED30A5CA96E.description: Identify, without counting, the number of objects in a collection of up to four objects (i.e., subitize).

71EAA47948F643A99D8FF0B6F6A1B969.description: Recognize and know the name of some written numerals.

0D948A918B5D441DAB78F391B80BF114.description: Recite numbers in order to twenty with increasing accuracy.

0AD7167A069A42C4A5AF00CB35B4514B.description: Children expand their under­ standing of numbers and quantities in their everyday environment.

5B11A87ACEF541FD87196803D1FBC31C.description: Solve simple addition and subtrac­ tion problems nonverbally (and often verbally) with a very small number of objects (sums up to 4 or 5).

29E9190888CF4D71B9BE7207B95A511C.description: Understand that putting two groups of objects together will make a bigger group.

5E6C6EC79EC84066AF76156C9D485E35.description: Understand that adding to (or taking away) one or more objects from a group will increase (or decrease) the number of objects in the group.

6025FC989EEF47F5BF72070E63263E9B.description: Compare visually (with or without counting) two groups of objects that are obviously equal or nonequal and communicate, “more” or “same.”

CAC3C1D4E681490487B4B6EBFD78DAB5.description: Children begin to understand number relationships and operations in their everyday environment.

82D4D0A2C92D4786BB88BE2292EDB392.description: Use the number name of the last object counted to answer the question, “How many . . . ?”

E426677069C6446C8485074F8C37B3F5.description: Count up to five objects, using one-to-one correspondence (one object for each number word) with increasing accuracy.

C53CC50AD0624EE7945FC2D6E85F91C0.description: Identify, without counting, the number of objects in a collection of up to three objects (i.e., subitize).

37213FC815E8441AAE0BD5D0513DB9BF.description: Begin to recognize and name a few written numerals.

C02C5AC935C7432BA776440BCB8F1003.description: Recite numbers in order to ten with increasing accuracy.

4DCEA30713494BFD8EE89E7858570F3B.description: Children begin to understand numbers and quantities in their everyday environment.

document.title: Science Content Standards for California Public Schools Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

D523F1395DBD4AD0B1A02456645CE425.description:
Identify changes in natural phenomena over time without manipulating the
phenomena (e.g., a tree limb, a grove of trees, a stream, a hillslope).

B9B93EA44FE3404D810D8D27C0F460F5.description:
Interpret events by sequence and time from natural phenomena (e.g., the relative
ages of rocks and intrusions).

7296476E92FD408EA975F3F4A2664BFC.description:
Read a topographic map and a geologic map for evidence provided on the maps
and construct and interpret a simple scale map.

FAB80D653D624060821233847B446162.description: Recognize whether evidence is consistent with a proposed explanation.

3EEFA561340E4D8389D5E62B21F7C1D5.description:
Communicate the steps and results from an investigation in written reports and
oral presentations.

3095AE502EA24D3085FE6723C053C2B5.description:
Construct appropriate graphs from data and develop qualitative statements
about the relationships between variables.

F8ABE52F116249CB9ED4DAA83531CEF6.description:
Select and use appropriate tools and technology (including calculators, computers,
balances, spring scales, microscopes, and binoculars) to perform tests, collect
data, and display data.

CED83A37F4744DCFA9A921F3E6E8460D.description:
Investigation and Experimentation: Scientific progress is made by asking meaningful questions and conducting careful
investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept and addressing the content
in the other three strands, students should develop their own questions and perform
investigations. Students will:

E626220DD563437682A9C6945A1CB39E.description: Students know the natural origin of the materials used to make common objects.

6FB31AA12F524EF194870DD393B01CAF.description:
Students know different natural energy and material resources, including air, soil,
rocks, minerals, petroleum, fresh water, wildlife, and forests, and know how to
classify them as renewable or nonrenewable.

3932658ED5574303AC4A737E9DDDB1D6.description:
Students know the utility of energy sources is determined by factors that are
involved in converting these sources to useful forms and the consequences of the
conversion process.

C910DA8A941E4FEDA215FECC4231AF11.description:
Resources:  Sources of energy and materials differ in amounts, distribution, usefulness, and the
time required for their formation. As a basis for understanding this concept:

43D2D8E1975245E992A4294B46FFE579.description:
Students know the number and types of organisms an ecosystem can support
depends on the resources available and on abiotic factors, such as quantities of
light and water, a range of temperatures, and soil composition.

BD79294219624517B389D23743FB6CFC.description:
Students know different kinds of organisms may play similar ecological roles in
similar biomes.

7CBF4377EAD14F1C8467D6121C02B1B3.description:
Students know populations of organisms can be categorized by the functions they
serve in an ecosystem.

F3CDDE650DB948D7B17C451A59E43450.description:
Students know matter is transferred over time from one organism to others in the
food web and between organisms and the physical environment.

FAAD800E7E3949E8B0CD81C6877A6F56.description:
Students know energy entering ecosystems as sunlight is transferred by producers
into chemical energy through photosynthesis and then from organism to organism
through food webs.

D48278934BF74D86836AB7A11EC87C2B.description:
Ecology: Organisms in ecosystems exchange energy and nutrients among themselves and
with the environment. As a basis for understanding this concept:

1C44F9F4A6C04575A1E86047FD54DED7.description:
Students know differences in pressure, heat, air movement, and humidity result in
changes of weather.

DF9B57AA85814D85AC2BE9744E2D71E4.description: Students know convection currents distribute heat in the atmosphere and oceans.

16F134A859E24698B5EED13A2138F667.description:
Students know heat from Earth’s interior reaches the surface primarily through
convection.

F9E6C4043D7642A6A5D26BCC234A1629.description:
Students know solar energy reaches Earth through radiation, mostly in the form of
visible light.

1205FA61241C4465869C23DEA28735E7.description:
Students know the sun is the major source of energy for phenomena on Earth’s
surface; it powers winds, ocean currents, and the water cycle.

EF382AA981F6427680477225D3615446.description:
Energy in the Earth's System: Many phenomena on Earth’s surface are affected by the transfer of energy through
radiation and convection currents. As a basis for understanding this concept:

845F8ACB0B89483F816C6E0E08A77A27.description:
Students know heat energy is also transferred between objects by radiation (radiation
can travel through space).

5EADD07B86FC467AA7CC45C1028CCD87.description:
Students know heat flows in solids by conduction (which involves no flow of
matter) and in fluids by conduction and by convection (which involves flow of
matter).

83C75FDF3BEF4E9486288BDADCAA7B2D.description:
Students know that when fuel is consumed, most of the energy released becomes
heat energy.

DCCC04E7251840AC96A65650403FFA83.description:
Students know energy can be carried from one place to another by heat flow or by
waves, including water, light and sound waves, or by moving objects.

5DB70EE20E7E4228B141CE2EBC939656.description:
Heat (Thermal Energy- Physical Sciences):  Heat moves in a predictable flow from warmer objects to cooler objects until all the
objects are at the same temperature. As a basis for understanding this concept:

E6A1AF9343C642F1BED572703309825B.description:
Students know earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, and floods change
human and wildlife habitats.

51CF892E55824679A51293C3E3CAC797.description:
Students know beaches are dynamic systems in which the sand is supplied by
rivers and moved along the coast by the action of waves.

1016EC88FD104FAF9FDA428CEBC25380.description:
Students know rivers and streams are dynamic systems that erode, transport
sediment, change course, and flood their banks in natural and recurring patterns.

1DDC3D7B96CE48E2AC7C7D0F1EFDF1B2.description:
Students know water running downhill is the dominant process in shaping the
landscape, including California’s landscape.

F03192A42B65414A870033A83A42E895.description:
Shaping the Earth's Surface: Topography is reshaped by the weathering of rock and soil and by the transportation
and deposition of sediment. As a basis for understanding this concept:

743E32E011C1454381AB1DD22EED3101.description:

the effects of an earthquake on any region vary, depending on the size of the
earthquake, the distance of the region from the epicenter, the local geology, and
the type of construction in the region.

mountains, faults, volcanoes) in terms of plate tectonics.

Students know major geologic events, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions,
and mountain building, result from plate motions.

11118C22F33C4EC0A6E2D999685D165D.description:
Students know that earthquakes are sudden motions along breaks in the crust
called faults and that volcanoes and fissures are locations where magma reaches
the surface.

8034AA771681421BB3CB372A106E44CF.description:
Students know lithospheric plates the size of continents and oceans move at rates
of centimeters per year in response to movements in the mantle.

4B131B700466487C90B7AB7F1B7F9C45.description:
Students know Earth is composed of several layers: a cold, brittle lithosphere; a
hot, convecting mantle; and a dense, metallic core.

events. As a basis for understanding this concept:

628B439406BF419E99250F7AD0054C02.description: The functions and properties of natural and designed objects and systems can be inferred from their overall structure, the way their components are shaped and used, and the molecular substructures of its various materials.

CA85F06A5E3B40288C925CFEE2AD2D2D.description: Changes of energy and matter in a system can be described in terms of energy and matter flows into, out of, and within that system.

6CA58F307C4C40BAB545B31DC5C186E5.description: The total amount of energy and matter in closed systems is conserved.

089418DD2C86457D827A249F5C39DCFF.description: In nuclear processes, atoms are not conserved, but the total number of protons plus neutrons is conserved.

04E1B9FD1EAF4D3DBF6AA4E8E93E34AA.description: Models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) can be used to simulate systems and interactions—including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales.

F9F6A1F13FE2429CA699446924189CEF.description: Models can be used to predict the behavior of a system, but these predictions have limited precision and reliability due to the assumptions and approximations inherent in models.

E921C0F20FE44045AE2B8ED9BD53A1A1.description: When investigating or describing a system, the boundaries and initial conditions of the system need to be defined and their inputs and outputs analyzed and described using models.

1D61B50DC2D94EB682ACC54527E6864C.description: The significance of a phenomenon is dependent on the scale, proportion, and quantity at which it occurs.

3A5008A02AAA40178D61BD47B315C1C2.description: Cause and effect relationships can be suggested and predicted for complex natural and human designed systems by examining what is known about smaller scale mechanisms within the system.

66FEA867997E46F3AFFAFA9EF6D21603.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena.

09AB81A95C9F418D88394603CF151B89.description: Humans depend on the living world for the resources and other benefits provided by biodiversity. But human activity is also having adverse impacts on biodiversity through overpopulation, overexploitation, habitat destruction, pollution, introduction of invasive species, and climate change. Thus sustaining biodiversity so that ecosystem functioning and productivity are maintained is essential to supporting and enhancing life on Earth. Sustaining biodiversity also aids humanity by preserving landscapes of recreational or inspirational value.

9B45E20BD0014D83A9CD7228F96ED68D.description: Biodiversity is increased by the formation of new species (speciation) and decreased by the loss of species (extinction).

E3D20D5ECAD94C9C95BF31E5C19BBDD3.description: Species become extinct because they can no longer survive and reproduce in their altered environment. If members cannot adjust to change that is too fast or drastic, the opportunity for the species' evolution is lost.

E96F7F0AF4E44583AA1F136EE97BAEDC.description: Changes in the physical environment, whether naturally occurring or human induced, have thus contributed to the expansion of some species, the emergence of new distinct species as populations diverge under different conditions, and the decline–and sometimes the extinction–of some species.

49AD83BEE42A4183BD7C220CAAC3D685.description: Adaptation also means that the distribution of traits in a population can change when conditions change.

6EC073D5D1014DDCA59A9E7CDD680F83.description: Natural selection leads to adaptation, that is, to a population dominated by organisms that are anatomically, behaviorally, and physiologically well suited to survive and reproduce in a specific environment. That is, the differential survival and reproduction of organisms in a population that have an advantageous heritable trait leads to an increase in the proportion of individuals in future generations that have the trait and to a decrease in the proportion of individuals that do not.

0A3310F1492C4ED8BB51C7B4F319151A.description: Evolution is a consequence of the interaction of four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for an environment's limited supply of the resources that individuals need in order to survive and reproduce, and (4) the ensuing proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in that environment.

ED923EF1614B4E2FA63EC03415FACB38.description: The traits that positively affect survival are more likely to be reproduced, and thus are more common in the population.

E012934EDAD148E29B7C86136DEBE8BB.description: Natural selection occurs only if there is both (1) variation in the genetic information between organisms in a population and (2) variation in the expression of that genetic information—that is, trait variation—that leads to differences in performance among individuals.

68BEEBB9FB984962B8C9536096AE7B08.description: Genetic information provides evidence of evolution. DNA sequences vary among species, but there are many overlaps; in fact, the ongoing branching that produces multiple lines of descent can be inferred by comparing the DNA sequences of different organisms. Such information is also derivable from the similarities and differences in amino acid sequences and from anatomical and embryological evidence.

8D46BDE058EB47448BD4B64D1EB9CED6.description: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

6F5CD0FACDB04D828150FA68C5BA18B8.description: Environmental factors also affect expression of traits, and hence affect the probability of occurrences of traits in a population. Thus the variation and distribution of traits observed depends on both genetic and environmental factors.

71A84E9CF4F64F9F8290AD303DA27C0B.description: In sexual reproduction, chromosomes can sometimes swap sections during the process of meiosis (cell division), thereby creating new genetic combinations and thus more genetic variation. Although DNA replication is tightly regulated and remarkably accurate, errors do occur and result in mutations, which are also a source of genetic variation. Environmental factors can also cause mutations in genes, and viable mutations are inherited.

EB7030FF09134E8FB97BA91E1EC10559.description: Each chromosome consists of a single very long DNA molecule, and each gene on the chromosome is a particular segment of that DNA. The instructions for forming species' characteristics are carried in DNA. All cells in an organism have the same genetic content, but the genes used (expressed) by the cell may be regulated in different ways. Not all DNA codes for a protein; some segments of DNA are involved in regulatory or structural functions, and some have no as-yet known function.

4DDC105123704D53AA6D114F105800D8.description: roup behavior has evolved because membership can increase the chances of survival for individuals and their genetic relatives.

A7200DAEFA71429D84DD1AA032DCAC0F.description: Moreover, anthropogenic changes (induced by human activity) in the environment—including habitat destruction, pollution, introduction of invasive species, overexploitation, and climate change—can disrupt an ecosystem and threaten the survival of some species.

EBE948E2F47E41F8981EEDAAD457EF73.description: A complex set of interactions within an ecosystem can keep its numbers and types of organisms relatively constant over long periods of time under stable conditions. If a modest biological or physical disturbance to an ecosystem occurs, it may return to its more or less original status (i.e., the ecosystem is resilient), as opposed to becoming a very different ecosystem. Extreme fluctuations in conditions or the size of any population, however, can challenge the functioning of ecosystems in terms of resources and habitat availability.

ACC8A0357BE14AF393402C968BD753DA.description: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are important components of the carbon cycle, in which carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, atmosphere, oceans, and geosphere through chemical, physical, geological, and biological processes.

EE5D2EBD71BB4B4E81A17D9A6379DFA8.description: Plants or algae form the lowest level of the food web. At each link upward in a food web, only a small fraction of the matter consumed at the lower level is transferred upward, to produce growth and release energy in cellular respiration at the higher level. Given this inefficiency, there are generally fewer organisms at higher levels of a food web. Some matter reacts to release energy for life functions, some matter is stored in newly made structures, and much is discarded. The chemical elements that make up the molecules of organisms pass through food webs and into and out of the atmosphere and soil, and they are combined and recombined in different ways. At each link in an ecosystem, matter and energy are conserved.

DFFC486DAE304C46833E1C0BFC58F95E.description: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration (including anaerobic processes) provide most of the energy for life processes.

48BAA48FA1EC4B6F8E12E2E10DF46967.description: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

4E92EBBA3E024CE1AC82C9644352D4EA.description: Ecosystems have carrying capacities, which are limits to the numbers of organisms and populations they can support. These limits result from such factors as the availability of living and nonliving resources and from such challenges such as predation, competition, and disease. Organisms would have the capacity to produce populations of great size were it not for the fact that environments and resources are finite. This fundamental tension affects the abundance (number of individuals) of species in any given ecosystem.

E9A7EFEA179043C68A8313EEC0C46936.description: As a result of these chemical reactions, energy is transferred from one system of interacting molecules to another. Cellular respiration is a chemical process in which the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and new compounds are formed that can transport energy to muscles. Cellular respiration also releases the energy needed to maintain body temperature despite ongoing energy transfer to the surrounding environment.

5B3EB3DB30EA45E8B8DF0962B0BFE3C3.description: As matter and energy flow through different organizational levels of living systems, chemical elements are recombined in different ways to form different products.

F25FA19CCA9F4CE7839D248A8AB938FB.description: The sugar molecules thus formed contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen: their hydrocarbon backbones are used to make amino acids and other carbon-based molecules that can be assembled into larger molecules (such as proteins or DNA), used for example to form new cells.

1B0A8AEFF5F747CF8C3F84C3AB3B5F5A.description: The process of photosynthesis converts light energy to stored chemical energy by converting carbon dioxide plus water into sugars plus released oxygen.

9CEED95B623141B7B209F4303DAFA9DA.description: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

AF483006B50A41C8BEA80AC8AE6F9A5D.description: In multicellular organisms individual cells grow and then divide via a process called mitosis, thereby allowing the organism to grow. The organism begins as a single cell (fertilized egg) that divides successively to produce many cells, with each parent cell passing identical genetic material (two variants of each chromosome pair) to both daughter cells. Cellular division and differentiation produce and maintain a complex organism, composed of systems of tissues and organs that work together to meet the needs of the whole organism.

AF28BA5153E04033A3F752459585524C.description: All cells contain genetic information in the form of DNA molecules. Genes are regions in the DNA that contain the instructions that code for the formation of proteins.

2D775E417D834671B12004F2E6C93C28.description: Feedback mechanisms maintain a living system's internal conditions within certain limits and mediate behaviors, allowing it to remain alive and functional even as external conditions change within some range. Feedback mechanisms can encourage (through positive feedback) or discourage (negative feedback) what is going on inside the living system.

DE94542ECE1542DA8709CC552CA76330.description: Multicellular organisms have a hierarchical structural organization, in which any one system is made up of numerous parts and is itself a component of the next level.

509ACD3928A24337A7AB28407100FCB1.description: All cells contain genetic information in the form of DNA molecules. Genes are regions in the DNA that contain the instructions that code for the formation of proteins, which carry out most of the work of cells.

ACC52556F6CA48F2A36A4C73CB574C78.description: Systems of specialized cells within organisms help them perform the essential functions of life.

D282746CE5244FA3A549A4039EE8125D.description: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.

5B0E6C6A68764B1783708F7413828B58.description: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.

FDAFA01BDC124916BBE734FE8DAD0692.description: Create or revise a simulation to test a solution to mitigate adverse impacts of human activity on biodiversity.

617745E6B55F4A08AF191E7B5EF99552.description: Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in: (1) increases in the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of other species.

71A093DF54C54BBD90561F143E09DD83.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.

05AF1C4555D34FC6981CBED122AC0D01.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait.

C50BB39BF21344BEAA4C835412A434E2.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.

F481FE58C22D446395A1D16AE36B59C6.description: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.

8038A0EF4FAB48099564C08608BA9452.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.

6036D6B5592B4527AEBFFA88CE24B88D.description: Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from: (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, and/or (3) mutations caused by environmental factors.

A6732EFED9214E7794196CD4F85B49B5.description: Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring.

2C3ECF377F694E69A0A9A7FD94B1E5D6.description: Heredity: Inheritance and Variation of Traits

C69589A8633B449FAE8EEB0440E95378.description: Evaluate the evidence for the role of group behavior on individual and species' chances to survive and reproduce.

F4EDDE1C635B46DAA0298E4E687AF0A6.description: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and biodiversity.

B1D5EFBEBC1C49CEACDE95F4317419B8.description: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning that the complex interactions in ecosystems maintain relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new ecosystem.

6BD010AFCBD649528FFF2B891966120A.description: Develop a model to illustrate the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.

C3CCFE7311194BE29FD2ACFE3C85D5DD.description: Use a mathematical representation to support claims for the cycling of matter and flow of energy among organisms in an ecosystem.

F390C9AE8C894107AB5DA10A88896D5B.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for the cycling of matter and flow of energy in aerobic and anaerobic conditions.

E37C62C2F62E48A998DA53F224F3570C.description: Use mathematical representations to support and revise explanations based on evidence about factors affecting biodiversity and populations in ecosystems of different scales.

89E9E121A3F945938B05822F21773C83.description: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.

759532A418AE44F886ACE49FDAD80B75.description: Use a model to illustrate that cellular respiration is a chemical process whereby the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and the bonds in new compounds are formed resulting in a net transfer of energy.

B2FF464B7C2B4A94A6A816C52A751928.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and/or other large carbon-based molecules.

7AA51065DC1B4F95A6D72DD298C744F2.description: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.

4E5F7A9AB4674E3FB1244C9E61655635.description: Use a model to illustrate the role of cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation in producing and maintaining complex organisms.

2FCC8878860A4B5BB003160E4F9FCAA1.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis.

FA31DF7AD73441D19AF27B23B8BD20F4.description: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.

761B10F7F0524B8198C27E1CEE95C1C8.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.

4D98F9CE4C3E460EBBBBB9940EFC345D.description: The process of making decisions about resources and natural systems, and how the assessment of social, economic, political, and environmental factors has changed over time.

D2F79E4B98E14122A559CD2E741F7A7B.description: There is a spectrum of what is considered in making decisions about resources and natural systems and how those factors influence decisions.

267DC9CE12644F12AA2F0F17F0990422.description: PRINCIPLE V: Decisions Affecting Resources and Natural Systems are Complex and Involve Many Factors Decisions affecting resources and natural systems are based on a wide range of considerations and decision‐making processes.

94C9D6741A744DD28884FAFE5C1A90E6.description: The capacity of natural systems to adjust to human-caused alterations depends on the nature of the system as well as the scope, scale, and duration of the activity and the nature of its byproducts

50DE416A622B4F6FA99245773C23D522.description: The byproducts of human activity are not readily prevented from entering natural systems and may be beneficial, neutral, or detrimental in their effect.

209B660F0E5D4FD3A3A283C4126DDC38.description: The effects of human activities on natural systems are directly related to the quantities of resources consumed and to the quantity and characteristics of the resulting byproducts.

6FA8D17960B74BC595A7A1FEEEEF3A39.description: PRINCIPLE IV: There are no Permanent or Impermeable Boundaries that Prevent Matter from Flowing Between Systems The exchange of matter between natural systems and human societies affects the long‐ term functioning of both.

F5F16073E6EE49BC98A450B98AF4B9A5.description: Human practices can alter the cycles and processes that operate within natural systems.

53AD2473116245E7BF43E1B87CB8D62E.description: Human practices depend upon and benefit from the cycles and processes that operate within natural systems.

AADA5EA8E0CE4B2CA6DB04BBC8F2A8B6.description: Natural systems proceed through cycles and processes that are required for their functioning.

9076AC8914B0413AAC8F8A1A157FE786.description: PRINCIPLE III: Natural Systems Change in Ways that People Benefit from and can Influence Natural systems proceed through cycles that humans depend upon, benefit from and can alter.

59056D667BF349B88DA6DCE6DDEAC38D.description: The legal, economic, and political systems that govern the use and management of natural systems directly influence the geographic extent, composition, biological diversity, and viability of natural systems.

FC69AE31C6874B2B8353ABB1317ED5EA.description: The expansion and operation of human communities influences the geographic extent, composition, biological diversity, and viability of natural systems.

63B2587F8F4E4C5299A5F42D996E8A7D.description: Methods used to extract, harvest, transport, and consume natural resources influence the geographic extent, composition, biological diversity, and viability of natural systems.

C97BF747DE2840C28747FB7E28177192.description: Direct and indirect changes to natural systems due to the growth of human populations and their consumption rates influence the geographic extent, composition, biological diversity, and viability of natural systems.

FCD907493A3A4C7AA33B7ACC58C6CEC8.description: PRINCIPLE II: People Influence Natural Systems The long‐term functioning and health of terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems are influenced by their relationships with human societies.

65C1E7EC2FA24EDEAAA5913FFE5D157D.description: That the quality, quantity, and reliability of the goods and ecosystem services provided by natural systems are directly affected by the health of those systems.

A49BE533D07244E3B203F2AF83E10EB4.description: The ecosystem services provided by natural systems are essential to human life and to the functioning of our economies and cultures.

79410833E7244A089802A34C08C542BD.description: The goods produced by natural systems are essential to human life and to the functioning of our economies and cultures.

A4C1653E1E5F46B8A3A20F40E31D14A3.description: PRINCIPLE I: People Depend on Natural Systems The continuation and health of individual human lives and of human communities and societies depend on the health of the natural systems that provide essential goods and ecosystem services.

695FDD6D796E49778C8DF838BBDD1FD8.description: Communicate scientific and/or technical information (e.g. about a proposed object, tool, process, system) in writing and/or through oral presentations

585F705C823648C89B35001013B3B71F.description: Evaluate data, hypotheses, and/or conclusions in scientific and technical texts in light of competing information or accounts.

8B23FB2A5DF749ABB9066FEF2C03E251.description: Gather, read, synthesize information from multiple appropriate sources and assess the credibility, accuracy, and possible bias of each publication and methods used, and describe how they are supported or not supported by evidence.

9FF0CE12266141FBAB2C41B800AC5F0C.description: Integrate qualitative and/or quantitative scientific and/or technical information in written text with that contained in media and visual displays to clarify claims and findings.

F07413FDFB014B7EB2E9DA62B4F808DA.description: Critically read scientific texts adapted for classroom use to determine the central ideas and/or obtain scientific and/or technical information to describe patterns in and/or evidence about the natural and designed world(s).

A5F18BC4F1ED4ECEB0A7B93CEAF60450.description:
Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information
Obtaining, evaluating, and communicating information in 6–8 builds on K–5 experiences and progresses to evaluating the merit and validity of ideas and methods.

D6166C1024A5493CA51B8CF4C8B17475.description: Evaluate competing design solutions based on jointly developed and agreed-upon design criteria.

F659ABB87F8F4F5BB8DC189B24B850DD.description: Make an oral or written argument that supports or refutes the advertised performance of a device, process, or system, based on empirical evidence concerning whether or not the technology meets relevant criteria and constraints.

25945EEF13EE4C069E44EB9FCC97E5E8.description: Construct, use, and/or present an oral and written argument supported by empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support or refute an explanation or a model for a phenomenon or a solution to a problem.

B77D61D5A78B4DB0BBCDC0CFF8BB18A7.description: Respectfully provide and receive critiques about one’s explanations, procedures, models and questions by citing relevant evidence and posing and responding to questions that elicit pertinent elaboration and detail.

96F49F99933F465DB131EF52DD8705E5.description: Compare and critique two arguments on the same topic and analyze whether they emphasize similar or different evidence and/or interpretations of facts.

0C6C3A35BDB44ADB99FD9891C3C1F432.description:
Engaging in Argument from Evidence
Engaging in argument from evidence in 6–8 builds on K–5 experiences and progresses to constructing a convincing argument that supports or refutes claims for either explanations or solutions about the natural and designed world(s).

945C104AF53D43C69C7B63F3E3F96E9B.description: Optimize performance of a design by prioritizing criteria, making tradeoffs, testing, revising, and retesting

499F8ACA8AE546438ADEA680485A7192.description: Undertake a design project, engaging in the design cycle, to construct and/or implement a solution that meets specific design criteria and constraints.

11474EC46E994D01826AE248707E228A.description: Apply scientific ideas or principles to design, construct, and/or test a design of an object, tool, process or system.

C02EDF85D5634015AAC6A45E149C93BD.description: Apply scientific reasoning to show why the data or evidence is adequate for the explanation or conclusion.

B271816BCD2C4DE1AD2226450FA80E29.description: Apply scientific ideas, principles, and/or evidence to construct, revise and/or use an explanation for realworld phenomena, examples, or events.

F47AD2FACB2C4B68A5D56121ADEE7A1A.description: Construct a scientific explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from sources (including the students’ own experiments) and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

B397254BCF5C4BF1BE5F47BD8B4695B0.description: Construct an explanation using models or representations.

B0CB46713B364999B384FFABF15A2002.description: Construct an explanation that includes qualitative or quantitative relationships between variables that predict(s) and/or describe(s) phenomena.

84CCADCF83B4446BBCD6AF8DF4C90D15.description:
Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions
Constructing explanations and designing solutions in 6–8 builds on K– 5 experiences and progresses to include constructing explanations and designing solutions supported by multiple sources of evidence consistent with scientific ideas, principles, and theories.

268D909696A841E08994EE19045DCAD1.description: Use digital tools and/or mathematical concepts and arguments to test and compare proposed solutions to an engineering design problem.

8ECB2A3E886E4945B9396C2CC2CCF74C.description: Apply mathematical concepts and/or processes (such as ratio, rate, percent, basic operations, and simple algebra) to scientific and engineering questions and problems.

7497CC437B704C41AA612954BDE977F7.description: Create algorithms (a series of ordered steps) to solve a problem.

BBC56E30ABAA462887D52A88A2A56615.description: Use mathematical representations to describe and/or support scientific conclusions and design solutions

005715FBC8D5487F8AF36C7D4B612345.description: Use digital tools (e.g., computers) to analyze very large data sets for patterns and trends.

D46DB3027DEA417F9E89EC20C821661E.description:
Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking
Mathematical and computational thinking in 6–8 builds on K–5 experiences and progresses to identifying patterns in large data sets and using mathematical concepts to support explanations and arguments.

353324C3B5EB45C89E95DE1DEB2EC9B3.description: Analyze data to define an optimal operational range for a proposed object, tool, process or system that best meets criteria for success.

ABA2D7F3F492451AAE5EC2776CB8F301.description: Analyze and interpret data to determine similarities and differences in findings.

37E31A2563CC447AA1A28F977CCB3D27.description: Consider limitations of data analysis (e.g., measurement error), and/or seek to improve precision and accuracy of data with better technological tools and methods (e.g., multiple trials).

22A5A0EEA2254F6CB1A902DD55B03576.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability (including mean, median, mode, and variability) to analyze and characterize data, using digital tools when feasible.

76F0D754075D4976BBEA8EA353EEEEFF.description: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence for phenomena.

C603F6369F8B4DD5B891A79D607EAB75.description: Distinguish between causal and correlational relationships in data.

04F55EE94CD2409084025EA862ADB348.description: Use graphical displays (e.g., maps, charts, graphs, and/or tables) of large data sets to identify temporal and spatial relationships.

30C192B70D41466ABE3A7E6FE1A79485.description: Construct, analyze, and/or interpret graphical displays of data and/or large data sets to identify linear and nonlinear relationships.

A3153508F5DF498A9B4B75975FEFEB59.description:
Analyzing and Interpreting Data
Analyzing data in 6–8 builds on K–5 experiences and progresses to extending quantitative analysis to investigations, distinguishing between correlation and causation, and basic statistical techniques of data and error analysis.

2E8F82280ED64483AFECF11F79D5304D.description: Collect data about the performance of a proposed object, tool, process, or system under a range of conditions.

863ECF7855EE4E928DA2DB637F83A39E.description: Collect data to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence to answer scientific questions or test design solutions under a range of conditions

5111218463AC4F778C2DBCFFEC79CC83.description: Evaluate the accuracy of various methods for collecting data.

F5AD93ACBD81466785AFEF2C851C2AAA.description: Conduct an investigation and/or evaluate and/or revise the experimental design to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence that meet the goals of the investigation.

827EA78995FD4457B5948F55E0A30162.description: Plan an investigation individually and collaboratively, and in the design: identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to do the gathering, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

3F81F45A01294FCC86770CB57D5F2B09.description:
Planning and Carrying Out Investigations
Planning and carrying out investigations in 6-8 builds on K-5 experiences and progresses to include investigations that use multiple variables and provide evidence to support explanations or solutions.

D7B65D2049AA44618E425F1B017A14A9.description: Develop and/or use a model to generate data to test ideas about phenomena in natural or designed systems, including those representing inputs and outputs, and those at unobservable scales.

C36C5DC0539D4D0FA2FD8FDAEAD8F4DF.description: Develop a model to describe unobservable mechanisms.

AF7B84592B764A39A85BC1399274F05E.description: Develop and/or use a model to predict and/or describe phenomena.

830C3E5FF35F4E768731BF131E3812DC.description: Develop and/or revise a model to show the relationships among variables, including those that are not observable but predict observable phenomena.

BA2138DB82EC44A6BCAAA391FAE23FAC.description: Use and/or develop a model of simple systems with uncertain and less predictable factors.

45118080584E4326ADF83B09DCEDC7C7.description: Develop or modify a model—based on evidence – to match what happens if a variable or component of a system is changed.

9F08D940439547E9A32B07D6455E93A3.description: Evaluate limitations of a model for a proposed object or tool.

BA269B35A0324987BB5A8298C8D0CCD3.description:
Developing and Using Models
Modeling in 6–8 builds on K–5 experiences and progresses to developing, using, and revising models to describe, test, and predict more abstract phenomena and design systems.

96291AFE6D204DB6B84A080AD7E0D18D.description: Define a design problem that can be solved through the development of an object, tool, process or system and includes multiple criteria and constraints, including scientific knowledge that may limit possible solutions.

12B55C2E8E6C48B2AEF8073F8ADC453F.description: Ask questions that challenge the premise(s) of an argument or the interpretation of a data set.

5DCF9616420642B3B5C4A84A23EA958B.description: Ask questions that require sufficient and appropriate empirical evidence to answer. * Ask questions that can be investigated within the scope of the classroom, outdoor environment, and museums and other public facilities with available resources and, when appropriate, frame a hypothesis based on observations and scientific principles.

9BBDD555F28F41FEB7B8A100A6575294.description: Ask questions * that arise from careful observation of phenomena, models, or unexpected results, to clarify and/or seek additional information. * to identify and/or clarify evidence and/or the premise(s) of an argument. * to determine relationships between independent and dependent variables and relationships in models.. * to clarify and/or refine a model, an explanation, or an engineering problem.

D49B5CADB7E1447CA84E98A6814747F7.description:
Asking Questions and Defining Problems
