8698DE26CD4D4CDBBF1A7D1DCD450744.description:
Describe and demonstrate how movement skills learned in one physical activity can be
transferred and used to help learn another physical activity.

7B9990D540DC4DD5BF9FC0CC911271F3.description:
Students demonstrate knowledge of movement concepts, principles,
and strategies that apply to the learning and performance of physical
activities.

800BEEF906A64BE1A88003986C6F3B59.description:
Create and perform a routine using fundamental gymnastic/tumbling skills, locomotor
and nonlocomotor movement patterns, and the elements of speed, direction, and level.

4FB65F85A8DF4F0FB9E8576861290C9D.description: Apply locomotor, nonlocomotor, and manipulative skills to team physical activities.

4B40CC10970346B8B2586A4C5885FF78.description: Demonstrate basic offensive and defensive skills and strategies in team physical activities.

0884038AF96746E485008F8898579ED3.description: Create and perform a square dance.

3DACD6A5150C4FA49317078EF0F53452.description: Identify and demonstrate square dance steps, positions, and patterns set to music.

1052A042B6D94A2CB6448296ED74BBA4.description:
Students demonstrate the motor skills and movement patterns needed
to perform a variety of physical activities.

57047E51EB894F06A20C5BF66F614A7E.description: Identify the responsibilities of a leader in physical activity.

095FF772CD284C1CB2AC35850B537A48.description:
Evaluate the effect of expressing encouragement to others while participating in a group
physical activity.

1375CD2FD3C040E6B94F7C8872D15C9E.description:
Demonstrate an acceptance of differences in physical development and personal
preferences as they affect participation in physical activity.

E004D92902A7452DBBD58FD62622F585.description:
Identify appropriate and inappropriate risks involved in adventure, individual, and dual
physical activities.

AF7D93D6B6BB47FA93D285E54BD9F61C.description:
Students demonstrate and utilize knowledge of psychological and
sociological concepts, principles, and strategies that apply to the
learning and performance of physical activity.

1024F481B7CD4F6E844297E29E0E298F.description: Discuss the effect of extremity growth rates on physical fitness.

C76B0AD1559246389C716491ACACFDB8.description: Explain progression, overload, and specificity as principles of exercise.

DE89E8DE73A44830BB0E40330C596970.description: Identify and apply the principles of overload in safe, age-appropriate activities.

E5EB00D209D44FDD8B115B9C24EA4F31.description: Describe the role of physical activity and nutrition in achieving physical fitness.

07A5CEF0D1654CB291D0356AFBC15BA2.description: Explain the effects of physical activity on heart rate during exercise, during the recovery phase, and while the body is at rest.

E1FBA50E95E94B79B0535D721DCBBC1F.description: Match personal preferences in physical activities with each of the five components of health-related physical fitness.

DF101E20FAE1437CB514B5254A18AC91.description:
Identify physical activities that are effective in improving each of the health-related
physical fitness components.

4A6D4CAFCB2841B7B517E61EC323BD0C.description: Develop a one-week personal physical fitness plan specifying the proper warm-up and cool-down activities and the principles of exercise for each component of health-related physical fitness.

80B66AF05D9B4CAAA95AB12D3B25B717.description:
Students demonstrate knowledge of physical fitness concepts,
principles, and strategies to improve health and performance.

B4168ED1F71644FBAE0FDF18B46102F4.description: Assess periodically the attainment of, or progress toward, personal physical fitness goals and make necessary adjustments to a personal physical fitness program.

79E0D612BBC14D3CADE32053C61111FD.description: Participate in moderate to vigorous physical activity a minimum of four days each week.

5B11E436E12B456E9C114B00433C1EB8.description: Plan a weekly personal physical fitness program in collaboration with the teacher.

6BFF1A22F4AB495FB65C88E300B4B2E0.description: Develop individual goals, from research-based standards, for each of the five components of health-related physical fitness.

A8B4E3A66F2442CD80F57EB895B58A37.description:
Evaluate individual measures of physical fitness in relationship to patterns of physical
activity.

F2EDED7A732E4C4AB40E820443DCF7F1.description:
Assess one’s own muscle strength, muscle endurance, aerobic capacity, flexibility, and
body composition by using a scientifically based health-related fitness assessment.

09FFE244BE854EE18B4637FB3B3D6225.description:
Students assess and maintain a level of physical fitness to improve
health and performance.

4D79A63CDB7E4CB3B30D1D4C9DB3790D.description: Develop an individual or dual game that uses a manipulative skill, two different offensive strategies, and a scoring system and teach it to another person.

C36EDCA912984D4E98F3037BBA06456A.description: Diagram and demonstrate basic offensive and defensive strategies for individual and dual physical activities.

667DB5709C3640A1B638DB0C12D26E6A.description: Compare and contrast the effectiveness of practicing skills as a whole and practicing skills in smaller parts.

BC16723C06D345059CD2754A7C166B76.description: Explain and demonstrate spin and rebound principles for performing manipulative skills.

230EB36C41224226AF4AAE6C586ED278.description:
Use principles of motor learning to establish, monitor, and meet goals for motor skill
development.

BCEEBA1F981A4954990CC47FCC8DFEFE.description: Analyze movement patterns and correct errors.

7B593F6A6FD844629D0B8C1F64386A5B.description: Identify and describe key elements in the mature performance of overhand, sidearm, and underhand throwing; catching; kicking/punting; striking; trapping; dribbling (hand and foot); and volleying.

441B074EC00E47B79E3B83C583304E3B.description:
Students demonstrate knowledge of movement concepts, principles,
and strategies that apply to the learning and performance of physical
activities.

DC4110D8BEC84431B06B1DA75E6B7EA6.description:
Demonstrate body management and object-manipulation skills needed for successful
participation in introductory adventure/outdoor activities.

7C66036380C74AB6A7296F4FB334B0CB.description:
Demonstrate body management and locomotor skills needed for successful participation
in track and field and combative activities.

A09B2D69CA494ED68571F43A83036CB1.description:
Demonstrate body management and object-manipulation skills needed for successful
participation in individual and dual physical activities.

E9507F39ED934E34A9821FD125F3F1B5.description: Combine manipulative, locomotor, and nonlocomotor skills into movement patterns.

6499B72ADBDB42BA94E448CAD2515575.description:
Demonstrate mature techniques for the following patterns: overhand, sidearm, and
underhand throwing; catching; kicking/punting; striking; trapping; dribbling (hand and foot); and volleying.

F408347482994F96BBE403DAD252C738.description:
Students demonstrate the motor skills and movement patterns needed
to perform a variety of physical activities.

document.title: California Common Core Math Standards

505E107CCF5846B9B827627660E8CB80.description: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.

C0E6DD7FB6EA493E95579FBAD01B82D3.description: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.

1DB721D0506A45208831DD164D25772B.description: Fit a linear function for a scatter plot that suggests a linear association.

0070BC29374A444481F3411EE5073A3A.description: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals.

6AA20FBE49E94FFCB8725594A2015DB4.description: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.

8636FF7B086D4F369C52BD7AB62A2474.description: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.

8F40EB311B324C4FAEFE5FEC91ADDA07.description: Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data.

449B5332E86C4263B106E39237027E22.description: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).

D9644706EC964DEE82C2701C68C24183.description: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.

4F89CF657D9E4A6F8D17F3307F12389D.description: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).

91A28D25D8904CA6ABC2FF249D65827F.description: Use coordinates to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles, e.g., using the distance formula.★

BA7CB004844F485FB29D08B597C6CEFD.description: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point).

5B5C6DED83274CCEB97608790F111814.description: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically. For example, prove or disprove that a figure defined by four given points in the coordinate plane is a rectangle; prove or disprove that the point (1, √3) lies on the circle centered at the origin and containing the point (0, 2).

121916C323204475907FD30421AC1FD0.description: Construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle.

34D2C6EC7386489099B2D9E8F8DB676C.description: Make formal geometric constructions with a variety of tools and methods (compass and straightedge, string, reflective devices, paper folding, dynamic geometric software, etc.). Copying a segment; copying an angle; bisecting a segment; bisecting an angle; constructing perpendicular lines, including the perpendicular bisector of a line segment; and constructing a line parallel to a given line through a point not on the line.

DD0287C429AB46CAAAC1A5FD96BF3973.description: Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.

710F681D8F414FBFA27A07161684D6C3.description: Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding pairs of sides and corresponding pairs of angles are congruent.

81D3E833FC974D1395CB9EE70817A710.description: Use geometric descriptions of rigid motions to transform figures and to predict the effect of a given rigid motion on a given figure; given two figures, use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to decide if they are congruent.

8965F405A5234FF0BF8D4DD75D36E063.description: Given a geometric figure and a rotation, reflection, or translation, draw the transformed figure using, e.g., graph paper, tracing paper, or geometry software. Specify a sequence of transformations that will carry a given figure onto another.

112DA3A87015499ABC5858D477377827.description: Develop definitions of rotations, reflections, and translations in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines, and line segments.

8AFE7E9535204F86A6B35E570C795DDC.description: Given a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, or regular polygon, describe the rotations and reflections that carry it onto itself.

556F3FDC589F47E7A0B39F42B1E473C9.description: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch).

7510B5F4EE0B4944B504F76DD3F55F98.description: Know precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line, and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line, and distance around a circular arc.

59F36B5E2B0544C6B516B628FD048BB7.description: Interpret the parameters in a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.

676DFC33ABDE42ACA022131A6C12A0D1.description: Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.

ADDE4E296017486E9FF906D74809D239.description: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).

D1F3C1E588394EF88D08FC361BD63FBE.description: Recognize situations in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval relative to another.

7A4196F446A04C6B8680C7242F32F4D8.description: Recognize situations in which one quantity changes at a constant rate per unit interval relative to another.

248C71D439714C5A830C5790AD5B9D37.description: Prove that linear functions grow by equal differences over equal intervals, and that exponential functions grow by equal factors over equal intervals.

A62C47C923AC4408A742089E9C517FB8.description: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.

A734808590DD4F09BBE6C50C2A3462A0.description: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing f(x) by f(x) + k, k f(x), f(kx), and f(x + k) for specific values of k (both positive and negative); find the value of k given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.

CABF690117124AB486EE2C87F8AA6183.description: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.★

2692AB9A3C894892825B38CC48D47F11.description: Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations. For example, build a function that models the temperature of a cooling body by adding a constant function to a decaying exponential, and relate these functions to the model.

59075EDDEC804A5E80F8DAB5454DB4ED.description: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.

C869C09203884456B8BDC5F0D332270E.description: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.

5B4A5F8582AD453A9824234E10E1C89A.description: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions). For example, given a graph of one quadratic function and an algebraic expression for another, say which has the larger maximum.

60A4DEE3CF6846A3928838EEBB0D97B8.description: Graph exponential and logarithmic functions, showing intercepts and end behavior, and trigonometric functions, showing period, midline, and amplitude.

67C2937E205A4B4A8ADA0B64CE3DDFFB.description: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.

EB4C0E27DAD34125AB8D5DE22D2AAA7C.description: Graph functions expressed symbolically and show key features of the graph, by hand in simple cases and using technology for more complicated cases.★

FC7682079E884E9AAE3645B74FD39FF7.description: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.★

7F89130D8A5F48B59F41CCC4838D06F3.description: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and, where applicable, to the quantitative relationship it describes. For example, if the function h(n) gives the number of person-hours it takes to assemble n engines in a factory, then the positive integers would be an appropriate domain for the function.★

3A56FFDD1A804B0DBE3D77D1C446B830.description: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negative; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity.★

36CF468F51B74A5694D0CCC8802438F9.description: Recognize that sequences are functions, sometimes defined recursively, whose domain is a subset of the integers. For example, the Fibonacci sequence is defined recursively by f(0) = f(1) = 1, f(n+1) = f(n) + f(n-1) for n ≥ 1.

72967E4D7B194219A678319E10BA83CF.description: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.

8D58D6CB611F428D9254B93869902519.description: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If f is a function and x is an element of its domain, then f(x) denotes the output of f corresponding to the input x. The graph of f is the graph of the equation y = f(x).

F5522BAC03DB4E3892B62F503E548978.description: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half- plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.

3E56A2BBE788427E9918F2EBE9F20E9F.description: Explain why the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs of the equations y = f(x) and y = g(x) intersect are the solutions of the equation f(x) = g(x); find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where f(x) and/or g(x) are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.★

5A166862B79D4D2281358DD2E905CCCD.description: Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane, often forming a curve (which could be a line).

3BACC442F95B4B2A85EF3F1CCE32E773.description: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.

79658A68AA304C7F8199153CCE37D0FC.description: Prove that, given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other produces a system with the same solutions.

89345CEA612141D7BB514A27619C45B7.description: Solve one-variable equations and inequalities involving absolute value, graphing the solutions and interpreting them in context. CA

81A75D08AF1B4DBD8FDAAA7CF8BFC434.description: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.

5BDDF6B3BAA64FD0AD70392ECA47817F.description: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify a solution method.

34C25D05334A4E30AC761D6B239D4C6B.description: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations. For example, rearrange Ohm’s law V = IR to highlight resistance R.

D926195BABA440979E162871BCB628EE.description: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or non- viable options in a modeling context. For example, represent inequalities describing nutritional and cost constraints on combinations of different foods.

66172CBC76484941B6AE976A8447694F.description: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.

FF138B9DBBC242A0B86FF31741F50856.description: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.

E5C2F80B0CAD48E691DBA0485403B8CA.description: Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity. For example, interpret P(1+r)n as the product of P and a factor not depending on P.

5B6680B8706D40F9B8835F39AFF64024.description: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

C18E4FA73FFB46DABD8524B45640002D.description: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context.

3D9D54BE522547709C3C5FF9847E13AA.description: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.

CCB40CD538E042EAA12C763E9488B538.description: Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.

9ADC8708BBD64F258B592A97636A9212.description: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.

document.title: Science Content Standards for California Public Schools Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

23F117F4A4A64FEFBBC5E9CD3DC81F7E.description: Know that when an observation does not agree with an accepted scientific theory, the observation is sometimes mistaken or fraudulent (e.g., the Piltdown Man fossil or unidentified flying objects) and that the theory is sometimes wrong (e.g., the Ptolemaic model of the movement of the Sun, Moon, and planets).

11AC32C7F1834B1AAC972CAEC4743EFB.description: Investigate a science-based societal issue by researching the literature, analyzing data, and communicating the findings. Examples of issues include irradiation of food, cloning of animals by somatic cell nuclear transfer, choice of energy sources, and land and water use decisions in California.

59CFC089FE79423FB21E00C26E8305CC.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining and applying concepts from more than one area of science.

103144F326BA41709F194309B3DCEB4D.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

DC69F0EEA14E40AE9634964410BBC475.description: Recognize the issues of statistical variability and the need for controlled tests.

E68216215F7F4DC0ADC5CFEA241B0998.description:
Analyze the locations, sequences, or time intervals that are characteristic of
natural phenomena (e.g., relative ages of rocks, locations of planets over time, and succession of species in an ecosystem).

C6D1AA5FB4C448DDB2920E668F474626.description: Read and interpret topographic and geologic maps.

2433E046AF8E4B18BF2D3728B8102928.description: Recognize the usefulness and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

84812217CABC4E41917FC5C200D1F956.description: Distinguish between hypothesis and theory as scientific terms.

ABBB370A703543A39A9DE15B5435148C.description: Solve scientific problems by using quadratic equations and simple trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

49933B1BFCBE4386B10A45E6DD0435DB.description: Formulate explanations by using logic and evidence.

9C8C9C8074654CAC8AC9C5CF7815EF97.description: Identify possible reasons for inconsistent results, such as sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

00AE20C66C74488CB06FAE9DA2B8721D.description: Identify and communicate sources of unavoidable experimental error.

EC63885E1A9241759BB53009429EE7C8.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology (such as computer-linked probes, spreadsheets, and graphing calculators) to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data.

35CE64064D4D42E4B3E674DE23575B0D.description: Scientific progress is made by asking meaningful questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept and addressing the content in the other four strands, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students will:

953EA26A0ED64008BAA52A483DFB8018.description: Students know how to analyze published geologic hazard maps of California and know how to use the map’s information to identify evidence of geologic events of the past and predict geologic changes in the future.

E076B9FF3CFE45D2B7EC3F65174EBAF2.description: Students know the importance of water to society, the origins of California’s fresh water, and the relationship between supply and need.

9D9EE490012A4A7BADD64CA8D582AD93.description: Students know the principal natural hazards in different California regions and the geologic basis of those hazards.

7AC4933A0B12410F85A649AF71DA7386.description: Students know the resources of major economic importance in California and their relation to California’s geology.

BE4A6E7E1BC94A7B9C5446B3B606C571.description: The geology of California underlies the state’s wealth of natural resources as well as its natural hazards. As a basis for understanding this concept:

6C97202912CF45BC9B97B702870C424D.description:
Students know the location of the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere, its role in
absorbing ultraviolet radiation, and the way in which this layer varies both naturally and in response to human activities.

1D8DB7D1FBBC468C8355BD6CA2D47171.description: Students know how the composition of Earth’s atmosphere has evolved over geologic time and know the effect of outgassing, the variations of carbon dioxide concentration, and the origin of atmospheric oxygen.

6BE299354A424EECA42B7BDA022D97D2.description: Students know the thermal structure and chemical composition of the atmosphere.

649E8C43CC9E4078A6501E15226B7BF2.description: Life has changed Earth’s atmosphere, and changes in the atmosphere affect conditions for life. As a basis for understanding this concept:

ABDC29161B6D44BF899A63EF97C3EE80.description: Structure and Composition of the Atmosphere

F9BCD3D26D264324A52AF14B8AEA489F.description: Students know the relative residence times and flow characteristics of carbon in and out of its different reservoirs.

296F4F328BE44A098BC0C5DF16A3BB70.description: Students know the movement of matter among reservoirs is driven by Earth’s internal and external sources of energy.

070468B58ABA461B901005A34E2E42EA.description: Students know the global carbon cycle: the different physical and chemical forms of carbon in the atmosphere, oceans, biomass, fossil fuels, and the movement of carbon among these reservoirs.

A0138AD440BE43769E7AB7005EB3D028.description: Students know the carbon cycle of photosynthesis and respiration and the nitrogen cycle.

8412B2C1BD7746FDA3C7520DEF716F70.description:
Each element on Earth moves among reservoirs, which exist in the solid earth, in oceans, in the atmosphere, and within and among organisms as part of biogeochemical
cycles. As a basis for understanding this concept:

F5996FB833034715AA59A610558B2AC6.description: Students know how computer models are used to predict the effects of the increase in greenhouse gases on climate for the planet as a whole and for specific regions.

A0EB4C67D084457195B14465FB469020.description: Students know how Earth’s climate has changed over time, corresponding to changes in Earth’s geography, atmospheric composition, and other factors, such as solar radiation and plate movement.

6164C86FF2CC46EA8C80E4DE5BC89A51.description: Students know the effects on climate of latitude, elevation, topography, and proximity to large bodies of water and cold or warm ocean currents.

DF75679F004E41A8B27F0580FD082819.description: Students know weather (in the short run) and climate (in the long run) involve the transfer of energy into and out of the atmosphere.

56F8C08EF8B74D9A9B9105337DAC565E.description: Climate is the long-term average of a region’s weather and depends on many factors. As a basis for understanding this concept:

2948F35DC7494499BAB12CCF7BA77799.description:
Students know features of the ENSO (El Niño southern oscillation) cycle in terms of
sea-surface and air temperature variations across the Pacific and some climatic results of this cycle.

D6FCA94065FD489A8CE0A35DE8C04217.description: Students know the interaction of wind patterns, ocean currents, and mountain ranges results in the global pattern of latitudinal bands of rain forests and deserts.

3C9481ADECFB40C584AEE2EBF740DE7E.description: Students know rain forests and deserts on Earth are distributed in bands at specific latitudes.

5A7E0856E50A4648BD37CE910863FE74.description: Students know properties of ocean water, such as temperature and salinity, can be used to explain the layered structure of the oceans, the generation of horizontal and vertical ocean currents, and the geographic distribution of marine organisms.

205A3E1CE9CB4609BFCFA2A0F06F4B5E.description: Students know the origin and effects of temperature inversions.

F5B03DE26C714F719F436FC4E5ACD304.description: Students know the relationship between the rotation of Earth and the circular motions of ocean currents and air in pressure centers.

C0D8132B5FE24A1587FE14F689A2F3D1.description: Students know how differential heating of Earth results in circulation patterns in the atmosphere and oceans that globally distribute the heat.

49E2244AE95444A5861BCDBD21756B20.description: Heating of Earth’s surface and atmosphere by the sun drives convection within the atmosphere and oceans, producing winds and ocean currents. As a basis for understanding this concept:

6AE21B723AB64280A6DBB28B7527E0CF.description: Students know the differing greenhouse conditions on Earth, Mars, and Venus; the origins of those conditions; and the climatic consequences of each.

07C891C30F8F4C78B291F478B41A31C5.description: Students know the different atmospheric gases that absorb the Earth’s thermal radiation and the mechanism and significance of the greenhouse effect.

61F59DE1B3824C2DB5AA135F3FF8EF56.description: Students know accelerators boost subatomic particles to energy levels that simulate conditions in the stars and in the early history of the universe before stars formed.

7A9FF1A64B124C2AB334675E39845B95.description: Students know that stars differ in their life cycles and that visual, radio, and X-ray telescopes may be used to collect data that reveal those differences.

323EBFDFD3244989A887DF53D4DE5DC0.description: Students know the evidence indicating that all elements with an atomic number greater than that of lithium have been formed by nuclear fusion in stars.

5DE821B80B8445ECBF9A55E893E54B83.description: Students know galaxies are made of billions of stars and comprise most of the visible mass of the universe.

46629A40EFEC4D62AC9CECD7398F4D5A.description: Students know the solar system is located in an outer edge of the disc-shaped Milky Way galaxy, which spans 100,000 light years. b. Students know galaxies are made of billions of stars and

2174D2F5288944DB9AAC5FDA9A976043.description: Students know the evidence for the existence of planets orbiting other stars.

F972ADD870004101BF4C96195BBAF2EE.description: Students know the evidence for the dramatic effects that asteroid impacts have had in shaping the surface of planets and their moons and in mass extinctions of life on Earth.

A9261BF0F01F4030AD0DCB2C88690960.description: Students know the Sun is a typical star and is powered by nuclear reactions, primarily the fusion of hydrogen to form helium.

182A627C4FC341DDB5B13C05C6980924.description: Students know the evidence indicating that the planets are much closer to Earth than the stars are.

AB5E94991DC3474698715E8AE29727BD.description: Students know the evidence from geological studies of Earth and other planets suggest that the early Earth was very different from Earth today.

5433079457E2423A8DB72A7D320FF70B.description: Students know the evidence from Earth and moon rocks indicates that the solar system was formed from a nebular cloud of dust and gas approximately 4.6 billion years ago.

68552632F06540A994F7C1C58FD7F374.description: Students know how the differences and similarities among the sun, the terrestrial planets, and the gas planets may have been established during the formation of the solar system.

018D156DF04549E88DDEB885327A956A.description: Astronomy and planetary exploration reveal the solar system’s structure, scale, and change over time. As a basis for understanding this concept:

58EAFC89AB5E4F8B85CACC165DC3B105.description: Communicate the steps and results from an investigation in written reports and oral presentations.

80F8B625C16F4DEB8F3B190A00BA2E9D.description: Construct scale models, maps, and appropriately labeled diagrams to communicate scientific knowledge (e.g., motion of Earth’s plates and cell structure).

9D00F5682FCE46B286A1FF3ADBC53589.description: Communicate the logical connection among hypotheses, science concepts, tests conducted, data collected, and conclusions drawn from the scientific evidence.

1DB811CBC36842A9AC540967E101B4E4.description: Use a variety of print and electronic resources (including the World Wide Web) to collect information and evidence as part of a research project.

EF362FFCD5274B92A31A4C27BB9CAC4D.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology (including calculators, computers, balances, spring scales, microscopes, and binoculars) to perform tests, collect data, and display data.

EA606CFEA7DF43F4974CCF9B1F659BC2.description: Students know how levers confer mechanical advantage and how the application of this principle applies to the musculoskeletal system.

F056A2E4393C482B85FABE536DADA727.description: Students know how to compare joints in the body (wrist, shoulder, thigh) with structures used in machines and simple devices (hinge, ball-and-socket, and sliding joints).

A181290943464BA7AC6D373A4C8A4DC4.description: Students know the angle of reflection of a light beam is equal to the angle of incidence.

8C02A560EED8412696A1885EC1C2B115.description: Students know light can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, and absorbed by matter.

ADB4D5A14F7841B188CAA2275BBBC0B7.description: Students know that white light is a mixture of many wavelengths (colors) and that retinal cells react differently to different wavelengths.

BD8D2004A78D43ACAB6403ABF11C0CF8.description:
Students know how simple lenses are used in a magnifying glass, the eye,
a camera, a telescope, and a microscope.

5CB74CBE85974D559A6D1CA28E7EFAA2.description: Students know light travels in straight lines if the medium it travels through does not change.

F461E0F007EB4E32879D87E619A6E577.description: Students know that for an object to be seen, light emitted by or scattered from it must be detected by the eye.

22FAC5EBE73F46B4990F6BF1E0117E7E.description: Students know visible light is a small band within a very broad electromagnetic spectrum.

09F6F1AD630E4B2EBA6C9BFDD943FC9D.description: Students know how to relate the structures of the eye and ear to their functions.

47D637E76F484B67AC1A8DD51B11BF0D.description: Students know the structures and processes by which flowering plants generate pollen, ovules, seeds, and fruit.

FBE44F2ACD1B4A8588E3B65D186A180F.description: Students know the function of the umbilicus and placenta during pregnancy.

CC41C7E2C73D433EA636E711DE9F2E2D.description: Students know how the reproductive organs of the human female and male generate eggs and sperm and how sexual activity may lead to fertilization and pregnancy.

C6CC1DA165D9461499FA4C386603566F.description: Students know how bones and muscles work together to provide a structural framework for movement.

42BFDDADF9F1445EB6F299714AE53C27.description: Students know organ systems function because of the contributions of individual organs, tissues, and cells. The failure of any part can affect the entire system.

6ECCFC6461F44958ABA421B9DAE28FA9.description: Students know plants and animals have levels of organization for structure and function, including cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and the whole organism.

79E53390EEE64B8C9168DAF9C253353E.description: Structure and Function in Living Systems - The anatomy and physiology of plants and animals illustrate the complementary nature of structure and function. As a basis for understanding this concept:

F038F2CB662F4452A204911AE99891FE.description: Students know how to explain significant developments and extinctions of plant and animal life on the geologic time scale.

51C0228E6AAE4FD2831A56F7C7544028.description: Students know how movements of Earth’s continental and oceanic plates through time, with associated changes in climate and geographic connections, have affected the past and present distribution of organisms.

9EA302AAA7A1444AB555290D737CF90E.description: Students know fossils provide evidence of how life and environmental conditions have changed.

0D4A54AFA9A84F43A031F74B9C6339A5.description: Students know that evidence from geologic layers and radioactive dating indicates Earth is approximately 4.6 billion years old and that life on this planet has existed for more than 3 billion years.

AD6205CBFE674413856BCC2A7DC9F047.description: Students know the history of life on Earth has been disrupted by major catastrophic events, such as major volcanic eruptions or the impacts of asteroids.

98D8FA4D8C3D4803B8B2E6DA92BB6489.description: Students know Earth processes today are similar to those that occurred in the past and slow geologic processes have large cumulative effects over long periods of time.

B86F53CA32574A64B8C9AE7DC4F2ECB2.description: Earth and Life History (Earth Sciences) - Evidence from rocks allows us to understand the evolution of life on Earth. As a basis for understanding this concept:

F777DC456C2D4EA8B9AE1212C9E20EB7.description: Students know that extinction of a species occurs when the environment changes and the adaptive characteristics of a species are insufficient for its survival.

CB0384AE9C6048098E3F5F7A9DBC58B9.description: Students know how to construct a simple branching diagram to classify living groups of organisms by shared derived characteristics and how to expand the diagram to include fossil organisms.

5C3C61EB407F4AECBE5A3DCE327411C2.description: Students know how independent lines of evidence from geology, fossils, and comparative anatomy provide the bases for the theory of evolution.

F2DEC440F2BB4314B5EB855D50550C39.description: Students know the reasoning used by Charles Darwin in reaching his conclusion that natural selection is the mechanism of evolution.

9A8454D47DFB4B76921FFAFC476FA0A6.description: Students know both genetic variation and environmental factors are causes of evolution and diversity of organisms.

17C8B1F1136A4AB0BFC0BAAF306000D0.description: Evolution - Biological evolution accounts for the diversity of species developed through gradual processes over many generations. As a basis for understanding this concept:

66B2AD1BA1474428BA88215801B9F05B.description: Students know DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the genetic material of living organisms and is located in the chromosomes of each cell.

38034B30A855467E9FFC910F8E29DFDE.description: Students know plant and animal cells contain many thousands of different genes and typically have two copies of every gene. The two copies (or alleles) of the gene may or may not be identical, and one may be dominant in determining the phenotype while the other is recessive.

5D57809D9675489D9A2D0DFFD6105E77.description: Students know an inherited trait can be determined by one or more genes.

7ADC7583AA944FDDA59ED4599E351084.description: Students know sexual reproduction produces offspring that inherit half their genes from each parent.

58C5CB4A080A4DB8B32B67F12686BEFD.description: Students know the differences between the life cycles and reproduction methods of sexual and asexual organisms.

F53CD76134EE48969D7DC6D1BA1E063F.description: Genetics - A typical cell of any organism contains genetic instructions that specify its traits. Those traits may be modified by environmental influences. As a basis for understanding this concept:

3771D43120FB4F9D8B270FDE9B451620.description: Students know that as multicellular organisms develop, their cells differentiate.

48E2A6E339434DE9A42571DA6AA0A530.description: Students know cells divide to increase their numbers through a process of mitosis, which results in two daughter cells with identical sets of chromosomes.

D9F2223B34504497B532BC3732F388FB.description: Students know that mitochondria liberate energy for the work that cells do and that chloroplasts capture sunlight energy for photosynthesis.

67CB9C0E6A5D42CC8123A57AB6110766.description: Students know the nucleus is the repository for genetic information in plant and animal cells.

ED61A933AA5A4E58B9C03628D7A4212B.description: Students know the characteristics that distinguish plant cells from animal cells, including chloroplasts and cell walls.

63A81C5F8F4C47299D756F1047980D45.description: Students know cells function similarly in all living organisms.

169F0C2ED88B4AFA9CD41C5C36F34024.description: Cell Biology - All living organisms are composed of cells, from just one to many trillions, whose details usually are visible only through a microscope. As a basis for understanding this concept:

fats, proteins, and DNA.

Students know how to use the periodic table to identify elements in simple
compounds.

7D67660C3BF44A27A47BA6D359C23BC1.description:
Students know atoms and molecules form solids by building up repeating
patterns, such as the crystal structure of NaCl or long-chain polymers.

4EBD434E822D4523B4D051E6DD6B843A.description: Students know a force has both direction and magnitude.

1EA191DF45C44E6C8CF3427FA970D60D.description: Motion - The velocity of an object is the rate of change of its position. As a basis for understanding this concept:

5772A19A893B4FEDAC541DFC2F444B16.description: Students know how to apply the concepts of electrical and gravitational potential energy to solve problems involving conservation of energy.

2E11CE63F05C47C48306CAA56C8DCE6F.description: Students know how to calculate the electric field resulting from a point charge.

C5AD67DFC6CC4FB19A03765576DA8309.description: Students know electric and magnetic fields contain energy and act as vector force fields.

591A4804B5034FF7A8EB44AC8D4D1BD0.description: Students know plasmas, the fourth state of matter, contain ions or free electrons or both and conduct electricity.

69964EE57992465E8C80779D05353ED5.description: Students know how to determine the direction of a magnetic field produced by a current flowing in a straight wire or in a coil.

2E1C970FF4F14E11B07EA9A5B807DB4D.description: Students know charged particles are sources of electric fields and are subject to the forces of the electric fields from other charges.

386860CBE5194C61944D5ADD4A5F8FA5.description: Students know any resistive element in a DC circuit dissipates energy, which heats the resistor. Students can calculate the power (rate of energy dissipation) in any resistive circuit element by using the formula Power = IR (potential difference) × I (current) = I2R.

742843E2CB8E44AB914A41E7A0BB85C8.description: Students know how to solve problems involving Ohm’s law.

EFA322FACDFE40ABB92EF31B354400B4.description: Students know how to predict the voltage or current in simple direct current (DC) electric circuits constructed from batteries, wires, resistors, and capacitors.

DE49FF75C1044828ABE947C2E0DB1669.description: Electric and Magnetic Phenomena - Electric and magnetic phenomena are related and have many practical applications. As a basis for understanding this concept:

CD0D85FC64DD47B1A6AAD6F89143C6CC.description: Students know radio waves, light, and X-rays are different wavelength bands in the spectrum of electromagnetic waves whose speed in a vacuum is approximately 3×10^8 m/s (186,000 miles/second).

543292F9DA8443A2A9B9324A95585F8D.description:
Students know sound is a longitudinal wave whose speed depends on the properties
of the medium in which it propagates.

756EE76CFC164ED3B1B3504733D398FC.description: Students know how to identify transverse and longitudinal waves in mechanical media, such as springs and ropes, and on the earth (seismic waves).

1B895513AC274F568BAE5DAB7EE436FE.description: Students know waves carry energy from one place to another.

A0DD6ED30BD14DEB9A6C8C13E50CA4C4.description: Waves - Waves have characteristic properties that do not depend on the type of wave. As a basis for understanding this concept:

20F4D422E8154EE19EBCDA2D83ED6DB3.description: Students know how to solve problems involving heat flow, work, and efficiency in a heat engine and know that all real engines lose some heat to their surroundings.

B5A1C5AA80D44412836E16944A8EB4E6.description: Students know the statement “Entropy tends to increase” is a law of statistical probability that governs all closed systems (second law of thermodynamics).

5F0070C143764434B7D816AACC4635B5.description: Students know that entropy is a quantity that measures the order or disorder of a system and that this quantity is larger for a more disordered system.

CEBA7B5348EB4D0EB0CF7F52C885D8A6.description: Students know that most processes tend to decrease the order of a system over time and that energy levels are eventually distributed uniformly.

CE71C192FDC24D999B7D0CC9E7EAAE51.description: Students know the internal energy of an object includes the energy of random motion of the object’s atoms and molecules, often referred to as thermal energy. The greater the temperature of the object, the greater the energy of motion of the atoms and molecules that make up the object.

F02AF898A3D54662A74AF2EB23BC51C7.description: Students know that the work done by a heat engine that is working in a cycle is the difference between the heat flow into the engine at high temperature and the heat flow out at a lower temperature (first law of thermodynamics) and that this is an example of the law of conservation of energy.

4B31C1D1DA9F4B04A44FE8FDBEB69464.description: Students know heat flow and work are two forms of energy transfer between systems.

17BC5DDC8A784B078CE41874F9575736.description: Students know how to solve problems involving conservation of energy in simple systems with various sources of potential energy, such as capacitors and springs.

F750DC08983F49E3BF79FE7E9A4B9AD8.description: Students know how to solve problems involving elastic and inelastic collisions in one dimension by using the principles of conservation of momentum and energy.

A2A933CE8C48467FBDD36CD4A3851C47.description: Students know an unbalanced force on an object produces a change in its momentum.

1087F39FD4554917AFFCDFD61808BA4A.description: Students know momentum is a separately conserved quantity different from energy.

9F9078F72CE64A7D98D3A978F597952B.description: Students know how to calculate momentum as the product mv.

E60DF514BB84492387148463D7D0ED4A.description: Students know how to solve problems involving conservation of energy in simple systems, such as falling objects.

4E1A2BF03D694DAFB4A1A9E250FE77CD.description: Students know how to calculate changes in gravitational potential energy near Earth by using the formula (change in potential energy) =mgh (h is the change in the elevation).

7DDD249F55504CA79C9FE40A21904FA7.description: Students know how to calculate kinetic energy by using the formula K.E. = 1/2 m v2.

29BE3486CA3C4261B78E9FAC938E3959.description: Conservation of Energy and Momentum - The laws of conservation of energy and momentum provide a way to predict and describe the movement of objects. As a basis for understanding this concept:

6A88DBB983E44679B0CC74E2E9D284F9.description: Students know how to solve problems involving the forces between two electric charges at a distance (Coulomb’s law) or the forces between two masses at a distance (universal gravitation).

298C7F1CEFDA448AAE121A33B2BE6494.description: Students know how to solve problems in circular motion by using the formula for centripetal acceleration in the following form: ac = v2/r.

9CDD9E589104427FA3AD278E758DC8E2.description: Students know how to solve two-dimensional problems involving balanced forces (statics).

25FE256C9DC3466682576A098524A322.description: Students know how to resolve two-dimensional vectors into their components and calculate the magnitude and direction of a vector from its components.

764145E4AA9A41D79E740BBB88C96F88.description: Students know how to solve two-dimensional trajectory problems.

A6DF308033074BAE830462DAF8BD60A7.description: Students know Newton’s laws are not exact but provide very good approximations unless an object is moving close to the speed of light or is small enough that quantum effects are important.

58BE2FB36BC8416785770FDB51118DB5.description: Students know circular motion requires the application of a constant force directed toward the center of the circle.

A2C501E987884CF18018319D6F2A86B5.description: Students know applying a force to an object perpendicular to the direction of its motion causes the object to change direction but not speed (e.g., Earth’s gravitational force causes a satellite in a circular orbit to change direction but not speed).

47D27EE0A91343839F65457168EB6619.description: Students know the relationship between the universal law of gravitation and the effect of gravity on an object at the surface of Earth.

1C64A86911F5457E9940E57A4BD1E9CE.description: Students know that when one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object always exerts a force of equal magnitude and in the opposite direction (Newton’s third law).

FBFDAFBF4BC746819EE6A1E7648CA4D0.description: Students know how to apply the law F = m·a to solve one-dimensional motion problems that involve constant forces (Newton’s second law).

4AA86688CC994802BBAA78CB53C3C2E5.description: Students know that when forces are balanced, no acceleration occurs; thus an object continues to move at a constant speed or stays at rest (Newton’s first law).

2C6E45CA0D71444C9B550C29967C2AF9.description: Students know how to solve problems that involve constant speed and average speed.

A90C6E64E1F440C99BD86B8350467901.description: Motion and Forces - Newton’s laws predict the motion of most objects. As a basis for understanding this concept:

document.title: Science Content Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

10B11814C2144497A51BB2C87F9E8883.description: Students know protons and neutrons have substructures and consist of particles called quarks.

B46552946A3441DDA591886266828189.description: Students know how to calculate the amount of a radioactive substance remaining after an integral number of half-lives have passed.

D8BA0FE7E99E450896203363D0A2F267.description: Students know alpha, beta, and gamma radiation produce different amounts and kinds of damage in matter and have different penetrations.

4918C2A56E4C49AF86A8C61F1E1EC04C.description: Students know the three most common forms of radioactive decay (alpha, beta, and gamma) and know how the nucleus changes in each type of decay.

EF6EDF687B464FBA81A12318AFF05B3E.description: Students know some naturally occurring isotopes of elements are radioactive, as are isotopes formed in nuclear reactions.

62C524CC91064777A56833D766E2FC1C.description: Students know the energy release per gram of material is much larger in nuclear fusion or fission reactions than in chemical reactions. The change in mass (calculated by E = mc^2 ) is small but significant in nuclear reactions.

B2E21350E0D549EA8B8717FB80628540.description: Students know protons and neutrons in the nucleus are held together by nuclear forces that overcome the electromagnetic repulsion between the protons.

4B5464A1D7C943569C8299D1C3F4B9D5.description: Nuclear Processes - Nuclear processes are those in which an atomic nucleus changes, including radioactive decay of naturally occurring and human-made isotopes, nuclear fission, and nuclear fusion. As a basis for understanding this concept:

049A6AEE5E224AE8BDDE4ECEEA7A110C.description: Students know the R-group structure of amino acids and know how they combine to form the polypeptide backbone structure of proteins.

9E50C781329545CE875F6A9DDB6B0A29.description: Students know how to identify the functional groups that form the basis of alcohols, ketones, ethers, amines, esters, aldehydes, and organic acids.

35539C07FE8E4913AE7CE53B2AA5F688.description: Students know the system for naming the ten simplest linear hydrocarbons and isomers that contain single bonds, simple hydrocarbons with double and triple bonds, and simple molecules that contain a benzene ring.

278171B171014D78AD55645514CBC135.description: Students know amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.

36B61D5DB541459083797090FFB901F5.description: Students know the bonding characteristics of carbon that result in the formation of a large variety of structures ranging from simple hydrocarbons to complex polymers and biological molecules.

55AF45C65E914A05B00279CE764602B4.description: Students know large molecules (polymers), such as proteins, nucleic acids, and starch, are formed by repetitive combinations of simple subunits.

7808C360813248D580E6BE92D2D6949B.description: Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry - The bonding characteristics of carbon allow the formation of many different organic molecules of varied sizes, shapes, and chemical properties and provide the biochemical basis of life. As a basis for understanding this concept:

F96AA37C0A4F42FFB3F15818D12FA3E0.description: Students know how to write and calculate an equilibrium constant expression for a reaction.

AE32E3789F264669A1ED688A6AD791AC.description: Students know equilibrium is established when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.

48663C48888E45BC9BD76CB4F3F9A49C.description: Students know how to use Le Chatelier’s principle to predict the effect of changes in concentration, temperature, and pressure.

24F3F030C3994984ADD73023EE4C30F1.description: Chemical Equilibrium - Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic process at the molecular level. As a basis for understanding this concept:

AB8D8667307D49988BC8A9FFDD0F6A69.description: Students know the definition and role of activation energy in a chemical reaction.

EB99D4CC87554F138C4F4C7425588BC1.description: Students know the role a catalyst plays in increasing the reaction rate.

1204007988D5428189992CD770402EF6.description: Students know how reaction rates depend on such factors as concentration, temperature, and pressure.

0558B8E6F66A4757AE2ABED36C6EE1A7.description: Students know the rate of reaction is the decrease in concentration of reactants or the increase in concentration of products with time.

530110D4C1ED49C185E24BD3BC50F3CE.description: Reaction Rates - Chemical reaction rates depend on factors that influence the frequency of collision of reactant molecules. As a basis for understanding this concept:

97BC89E98EF04D8AA0B5CCCC330EE059.description: Students know how to use the Gibbs free energy equation to determine whether a reaction would be spontaneous.

DD373B354F804CD3BF796AB9D3AD8E05.description: Students know how to apply Hess’s law to calculate enthalpy change in a reaction.

7DA0EE8DE6914E2AB9B8713690D85E8A.description: Students know how to solve problems involving heat flow and temperature changes, using known values of specific heat and latent heat of phase change.

E4F111AC51F244AA9FE58488C823EDA0.description: Students know energy is released when a material condenses or freezes and is absorbed when a material evaporates or melts.

71A75B2126454BEDBF3A5CA0B126C617.description: Students know chemical processes can either release (exothermic) or absorb (endothermic) thermal energy.

41A40B4F82B44F70A7A87EFED6E9F32A.description: Students know how to describe temperature and heat flow in terms of the motion of molecules (or atoms).

EB7CE72D18DC434E85C4C7586DF93114.description: Chemical Thermodynamics - Energy is exchanged or transformed in all chemical reactions and physical changes of matter. As a basis for understanding this concept:

016CDA2E069141938C2D7372BE647C6B.description: Students know how molecules in a solution are separated or purified by the methods of chromatography and distillation.

66FB586D863649C9B702A9CC196C723D.description: Students know the relationship between the molality of a solute in a solution and the solution’s depressed freezing point or elevated boiling point.

8B55A69207C54B50BDEEB06C3D6BE45B.description: Students know how to calculate the concentration of a solute in terms of grams per liter, molarity, parts per million, and percent composition.

14311E0236CC4ABFB76CC8E33DCCE252.description: Students know temperature, pressure, and surface area affect the dissolving process.

371F8B630E4846EF9E010ECE4C596582.description: Students know how to describe the dissolving process at the molecular level by using the concept of random molecular motion.

D58D9CC451924308838CCBB6702524C7.description: Students know the definitions of solute and solvent.

F280D8D199AC42C3BCB65FDB81C01E8C.description: Solutions - Solutions are homogeneous mixtures of two or more substances. As a basis for understanding this concept:

D37DB661290D406189981EF4A685B1A9.description: Students know buffers stabilize pH in acid–base reactions.

38BCD49DFD5242138B57A42885F73F43.description: Students know how to calculate pH from the hydrogen-ion concentration.

3AD1CBB6B65647D088577F5364A61AA7.description: Students know the Arrhenius, Brønsted-Lowry, and Lewis acid–base definitions.

508FCFF7C715400886F33972B49C185D.description: Students know how to use the pH scale to characterize acid and base solutions.

B8AF30737F574B6083F48751A0F32303.description: Students know strong acids and bases fully dissociate and weak acids and bases partially dissociate.

F8F95BBE9C1D4AD4AF1BA9D89CF3A708.description: Students know acids are hydrogen-ion-donating and bases are hydrogen-ion-accepting substances.

90A4B25E9E7B43B5A68808DF3E1F156E.description: Students know the observable properties of acids, bases, and salt solutions.

738615B25E1F499FA40C2B7E94A4D58C.description: Acids and Bases - Acids, bases, and salts are three classes of compounds that form ions in water solutions. As a basis for understanding this concept:

B53DF41253B942C5AC4671C63CA6C0CB.description: Students know how to apply Dalton’s law of partial pressures to describe the composition of gases and Graham’s law to predict diffusion of gases.

FFF7FF8E02624604B60EF9E1A9095CD5.description: Students know how to solve problems by using the ideal gas law in the form PV = nRT.

829077D9EEA043DA9FB01550BCB30DDE.description: Students know the kinetic theory of gases relates the absolute temperature of a gas to the average kinetic energy of its molecules or atoms.

FCDB0DA46BC849939147247BFD4C085F.description: Students know there is no temperature lower than 0 Kelvin.

0FEDC7E79E524CDD991FAA66F24B30F2.description: Students know how to convert between the Celsius and Kelvin temperature scales.

FC7A853E86F64BE2A9FC16FC066E6EEB.description: Students know the values and meanings of standard temperature and pressure (STP).

86244859DBDC413B95C87D505B7D3B51.description: Students know how to apply the gas laws to relations between the pressure, temperature, and volume of any amount of an ideal gas or any mixture of ideal gases.

6339E353C6F34F378DA9DC65A0D7C6C1.description: Students know the random motion of molecules explains the diffusion of gases.

DE2B7B28D4464082AF6C17143918D2A4.description: Students know the random motion of molecules and their collisions with a surface create the observable pressure on that surface.

2F159FADB9C8462F88F79C8566C054BB.description: Gases and Their Properties - The kinetic molecular theory describes the motion of atoms and molecules and explains the properties of gases. As a basis for understanding this concept:

880D9053082A4EDC85CDC02F81ED4109.description: Students know how to identify reactions that involve oxidation and reduction and how to balance oxidation-reduction reactions.

C803FAE51D3A46DCAA92CF248A58511D.description: Students know how to calculate percent yield in a chemical reaction.

91C10ED3920746BF8A39EC9FD3448256.description: Students know how to calculate the masses of reactants and products in a chemical reaction from the mass of one of the reactants or products and the relevant atomic masses.

1510BCAC44C641EA87A9859F8D22E476.description: Students know how to determine the molar mass of a molecule from its chemical formula and a table of atomic masses and how to convert the mass of a molecular substance to moles, number of particles, or volume of gas at standard temperature and pressure.

0C3AE49D950A4154BFEFE15611628F7F.description: Students know one mole equals 6.02 x 10^23 particles (atoms or molecules).

AE71333122F64A299BE53B16A009535E.description: Students know the quantity one mole is set by defining one mole of carbon 12 atoms to have a mass of exactly 12 grams.

995FA352DA4F4A4D9832EFC5874BEE94.description: Students know how to describe chemical reactions by writing balanced equations.

61B0DE31A1A343158BB86656DA47D43D.description: Conservation of Matter and Stoichiometry - The conservation of atoms in chemical reactions leads to the principle of conservation of matter and the ability to calculate the mass of products and reactants. As a basis for understanding this concept:

B4BBD041E0174EA39AC14BA3FF0BDCC8.description:
Students know how to identify solids and liquids held together by van der Waals
forces or hydrogen bonding and relate these forces to volatility and boiling/ melting point temperatures.

59D828453AAF4D0A822B654B6C51C51F.description: Students know how electronegativity and ionization energy relate to bond formation.

E68C386716194542B28D4D7BBD343E1A.description: Students know how to predict the shape of simple molecules and their polarity from Lewis dot structures.

EB8F567E0BAE4DDDBC6018BF9037BDA6.description: Students know how to draw Lewis dot structures.

2BF9C6DB5AD9479AAFD2F45DE38D7F47.description: Students know the atoms and molecules in liquids move in a random pattern relative to one another because the intermolecular forces are too weak to hold the atoms or molecules in a solid form.

29231274C4D0439CAEDD246FE3175927.description: Students know salt crystals, such as NaCl, are repeating patterns of positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction.

BBFB18DFD5CE44EE8D803ACA0C131458.description: Students know chemical bonds between atoms in molecules such as H2 , CH4 , NH3 , H2 CCH2 , N2 , Cl2 , and many large biological molecules are covalent.

6B24F03981CB4CBB9777686D5484A459.description: Students know atoms combine to form molecules by sharing electrons to form covalent or metallic bonds or by exchanging electrons to form ionic bonds.

BA7C1030CFEA4833A006E4A4C30FC5DC.description: Chemical Bonds - Biological, chemical, and physical properties of matter result from the ability of atoms to form bonds from electrostatic forces between electrons and protons and between atoms and molecules. As a basis for understanding this concept:

FE26FF9938C241C4B7338C0D3E1CCDD0.description: Students know that spectral lines are the result of transitions of electrons between energy levels and that these lines correspond to photons with a frequency related to the energy spacing between levels by using Planck’s relationship = hv).

5D811A14B0104F4C9CD0461DEEEC8961.description: Students know the experimental basis for the development of the quantum theory of atomic structure and the historical importance of the Bohr model of the atom.

B0E6E2CF43824014BB4A8C7D3BADACD6.description: Students know the experimental basis for Thomson’s discovery of the electron, Rutherford’s nuclear atom, Millikan’s oil drop experiment, and Einstein’s explanation of the photoelectric effect.

AF5F714B9C5340AAB9C333B25E92CF46.description: Students know how to relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its quantum electron configuration and to its reactivity with other elements in the table.

12FAF72DCEC94FE881C298EC370B6B89.description: Students know how to use the periodic table to identify the lanthanide, actinide, and transactinide elements and know that the transuranium elements were synthesized and identified in laboratory experiments through the use of nuclear accelerators.

276FE0E8E68247C18043DF8D0D9B4C5B.description: Students know the nucleus of the atom is much smaller than the atom yet contains most of its mass.

D7A1E3965E344977BBB32BE4E4A7E51C.description: Students know how to use the periodic table to determine the number of electrons available for bonding.

9B4E13B1B961473CAB004962C55F4DDF.description: Students know how to use the periodic table to identify alkali metals, alkaline earth metals and transition metals, trends in ionization energy, electronegativity, and the relative sizes of ions and atoms.

C2F30A72C4E04C4FA533958FBB0EF25C.description: Students know how to use the periodic table to identify metals, semimetals, nonmetals, and halogens.

2D0FF6215C1B479F8DD355C70AF694D1.description: Students know how to relate the position of an element in the periodic table to its atomic number and atomic mass.

8BC99A1F26BD46509D64EA814B953324.description: Atomic and Molecular Structure - The periodic table displays the elements in increasing atomic number and shows how periodicity of the physical and chemical properties of the elements relates to atomic structure. As a basis for understanding this concept:

document.title: Science Content Standards for California Public Schools, Kindergarten Through Grade Twelve

CCA32DA9A7044BCB98842AC6659FF295.description: Students know the roles of phagocytes, B-lymphocytes, and T-lymphocytes in the immune system.

926483CA4EC64CA4B340D94E3E8221C4.description: Students know why an individual with a compromised immune system (for example, a person with AIDS) may be unable to fight off and survive infections by microorganisms that are usually benign.

47FFC99B6E304BE9B23E87B99630B4A5.description: Students know there are important differences between bacteria and viruses with respect to their requirements for growth and replication, the body’s primary defenses against bacterial and viral infections, and effective treatments of these infections.

52F46EBD4C1445AD915A3E381D5ECCDB.description: Students know how vaccination protects an individual from infectious diseases.

27B83D6CD3AB4AF0B93E203B83617B20.description: Students know the role of antibodies in the body’s response to infection.

78C043DF282E411B901AA9A3272E8D56.description: Students know the role of the skin in providing nonspecific defenses against infection.

EA6B3D878A7B440EA1BCCC28EA6FC9D6.description: Physiology - Organisms have a variety of mechanisms to combat disease. As a basis for under-standing the human immune response:

2F82375C30F548C8B0DFDDF274696FE2.description: Students know how hormones (including digestive, reproductive, osmoregulatory) provide internal feedback mechanisms for homeostasis at the cellular level and in whole organisms.

B62A342BFA804611A46196B621B48F98.description: Students know the cellular and molecular basis of muscle contraction, including the roles of actin, myosin, Ca+2, and ATP.

23903CFBC54E4A6A8E87B6E64BCB8816.description: Students know the homeostatic role of the kidneys in the removal of nitrogenous wastes and the role of the liver in blood detoxification and glucose balance.

04DA31EA53E64807A39AC3C4DF172FCB.description: Students know the individual functions and sites of secretion of digestive enzymes (amylases, proteases, nucleases, lipases), stomach acid, and bile salts.

ADC3B8AFCB3147ED805715963FDCF091.description: Students know the roles of sensory neurons, interneurons, and motor neurons in sensation, thought, and response.

4B079F24201741D2B7701A8AA3204DE2.description: Students know the functions of the nervous system and the role of neurons in transmitting electrochemical impulses.

CA7935811E584E44AF7114D764318F91.description: Students know how feedback loops in the nervous and endocrine systems regulate conditions in the body.

5BCAF38214F846A6AA7B82B379D0294A.description:
Students know how the nervous system mediates communication between different
parts of the body and the body’s interactions with the environment.

BC036E9C7B164CDCAE9CFB7772EC497B.description: Students know how the complementary activity of major body systems provides cells with oxygen and nutrients and removes toxic waste products such as carbon dioxide.

E10B4727E4C54D668530AE66E96194BD.description: Physiology - As a result of the coordinated structures and functions of organ systems, the internal environment of the human body remains relatively stable (homeostatic) despite changes in the outside environment. As a basis for understanding this concept:

516DD668EE7D4A308EDB9FFD879D34A0.description:
Students know how several independent molecular clocks, calibrated against each other and combined with evidence from the fossil record, can help to estimate
how long ago various groups of organisms diverged evolutionarily from one another.

0C62997D1D634DD9851AA307591795EC.description: Students know how to use comparative embryology, DNA or protein sequence comparisons, and other independent sources of data to create a branching diagram (cladogram) that shows probable evolutionary relationships.

F377966DD82C44BDBBFEB050B170632E.description: Students know how to analyze fossil evidence with regard to biological diversity, episodic speciation, and mass extinction.

247B8489930D45389051BBDB27EBA806.description: Students know reproductive or geographic isolation affects speciation.

C696B9A9908644548D6CC210EB9B41F4.description: Students know the effects of genetic drift on the diversity of organisms in a population.

9C3C2D3461C3482AB7239B1EB16E7704.description: Students know a great diversity of species increases the chance that at least some organisms survive major changes in the environment.

D4E9EBBCBFE64F1E8A6C4EB69E8C74CB.description: Students know how natural selection determines the differential survival of groups of organisms.

9D4C929EE370428C85F8ACEFD6B72DB4.description: Evolution - Evolution is the result of genetic changes that occur in constantly changing environments. As a basis for understanding this concept:

7431F6E8B34143448EB52623359B7F7D.description: Students know how to solve the Hardy-Weinberg equation to predict the frequency of genotypes in a population, given the frequency of phenotypes.

8D9B5CB4756C4570B5EC3139A5B2AD2F.description: Students know the conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in a population and why these conditions are not likely to appear in nature.

211F1787B86E449BB1A429464F6227A6.description:
Students know variation within a species increases the likelihood that at least
some members of a species will survive under changed environmental conditions.

E1374CCE89184D7487191471805B0ED1.description: Students know new mutations are constantly being generated in a gene pool.

5D3AB02B944745C4B63BB88811AC8C39.description: Students know why alleles that are lethal in a homozygous individual may be carried in a heterozygote and thus maintained in a gene pool.

B85323AC19434622B132D72E0407809D.description: Students know why natural selection acts on the phenotype rather than the genotype of an organism.

523AE6D9D61740E2AB6CADC5AF75FA6A.description: Evolution - The frequency of an allele in a gene pool of a population depends on many factors and may be stable or unstable over time. As a basis for understanding this concept:

2C511327EB9E428196FC0A846AE19A50.description: Students know how to distinguish between the accommodation of an individual organism to its environment and the gradual adaptation of a lineage of organisms through genetic change.

B84AB1137CEE4E24809905291842AA4A.description: Students know at each link in a food web some energy is stored in newly made structures but much energy is dissipated into the environment as heat. This dissipation may be represented in an energy pyramid.

DA3ABA88CF104B55B590785F8E3E2099.description: Students know a vital part of an ecosystem is the stability of its producers and decomposers.

A4563F4DDCE74424878A22EBC73C5359.description: Students know how water, carbon, and nitrogen cycle between abiotic resources and organic matter in the ecosystem and how oxygen cycles through photosynthesis and respiration.

B3815730877540A6B7D50256620FF49B.description: Students know how fluctuations in population size in an ecosystem are determined by the relative rates of birth, immigration, emigration, and death.

287A353264E34392A8ECBEA7B798AE5A.description: Students know how to analyze changes in an ecosystem resulting from changes in climate, human activity, introduction of nonnative species, or changes in population size.

623C643F51784141B1F082F042047E5C.description: Students know biodiversity is the sum total of different kinds of organisms and is affected by alterations of habitats.

26364CD92938447EBD81678FCB8DF684.description: Ecology - Stability in an ecosystem is a balance between competing effects. As a basis for understanding this concept:

C62565ECB84B4CD8A4F33C55DA235FD7.description: Students know how exogenous DNA can be inserted into bacterial cells to alter their genetic makeup and support expression of new protein products.

D32A11D8BF41450FA128E06C8BC2E18C.description: Students know how basic DNA technology (restriction digestion by endonucleases, gel electrophoresis, ligation, and transformation) is used to construct recombinant DNA molecules.

92BBB315E5A64EF4B65786BE22FB4607.description: Students know how genetic engineering (biotechnology) is used to produce novel biomedical and agricultural products.

119FD66736434B2C832B730625FC750D.description: Students know how to apply base-pairing rules to explain precise copying of DNA during semiconservative replication and transcription of information from DNA into mRNA.

3FABBD59B74B484A874DA4C99C2F2771.description: Students know the general structures and functions of DNA, RNA, and protein.

8C227644FD2D4E4FA8DE818ACD45B6BA.description: Genetics - The genetic composition of cells can be altered by incorporation of exogenous DNA into the cells. As a basis for understanding this concept:

96EC89896FB7420DB4B2015760E3C2CC.description: Students know why proteins having different amino acid sequences typically have different shapes and chemical properties.

6DD69831F1314AB88634D3AB3C97CF76.description: Students know proteins can differ from one another in the number and sequence of amino acids.

D6FFC59572DC4903A407087A3F7B9D5E.description: Students know specialization of cells in multicellular organisms is usually due to different patterns of gene expression rather than to differences of the genes themselves.

96B5DACF8D8B443AB0E6343565A3281D.description:
How did other societies (the Greeks, Hellenistic states, Han China, Parthian
Persia) influence and affect the Romans?

What were the strengths and weaknesses of the Roman Republic? Why did
the Roman Republic fall?

Buddhism, and the connections between China and other regions of
Afroeurasia?

powerful?

rulers, and societies?

how did the connections between the Indian subcontinent and other regions
of Afroeurasia increase?

Hinduism, support individuals, rulers, and societies?

civilization?

Alexander the Great and the spread of Hellenistic culture, affect increasing
connections among regions in Afroeurasia?

emphasis on reason and intellectual development, and historical, scientific,
and literary forms) support individuals, states, and societies?

the achievements and limitations of Athenian democracy?

Persians and the Greeks, and between Athenians and Spartans?

coast, and the surrounding seas affect the development of Greek societies?

did the religious practices of Judaism change and develop over time?

How did civilizations—complex urban societies—develop in Mesopotamia,
Egypt, and Kush?

Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Kush

were the effects of these new ways of life?

Development of Human Societies

connections between societies increase over time?

How did the major religious and
philosophical systems (Judaism,
Greek thought, Hinduism, Buddhism,
Confucianism) support individuals,
rulers, and societies?

(hunting and gathering, agriculture,
civilizations, urban societies, states, and
empires), and how did they change over time?

How did the environment influence
human migration, ancient ways of life,
and the development of societies?
